subject: ss-critical-care
title: Critical Care Medicine
curriculum: NMC competency-based DM Critical Care Medicine, at NEET-SS depth. This group is not a feeder-speciality paper.
examPattern: NEET-SS Critical Care Medicine group (NBEMS pattern in force for the 2025 and 2026 cycles): one computer-based paper of 150 MCQs in 150 minutes, in three time-bound sections of 50 questions and 50 minutes. Marking is +4 for a correct answer and -1 for a wrong answer. Unlike the Medical group, the Critical Care Medicine paper is drawn from Critical Care Medicine itself, not from a general-medicine feeder paper. Eligible feeder degrees are those listed in the current NBEMS information bulletin annexure. This blueprint stays at that exit-exam depth and does not add operative ECMO or full DrNB training topics.
book: Marino, The ICU Book 5th Edition (2025); Washington Manual of Critical Care 4th Edition (2025); Chang, Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation 4th Edition (waveform and mode principles); Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22nd Edition where a critical-care chapter is thin

topics.title: Oxygen delivery and tissue oxygenation
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 9 Systemic Oxygenation; Ch. 12 Anemia and Red Blood Cell Transfusions

mustKnow.fact: Arterial oxygen content equals 1.34 times haemoglobin times arterial saturation, plus 0.003 times PaO2. The dissolved fraction is small, so haemoglobin and saturation decide content.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 9

mustKnow.fact: Oxygen delivery is cardiac output times arterial content. Oxygen uptake is cardiac output times the arterial to venous content difference. The normal oxygen extraction ratio is about 25%, and mixed venous saturation is about 65% to 75%.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 9

mustKnow.fact: Central venous oxygen saturation is not the same measurement as mixed venous saturation. A low central venous saturation still means delivery is short of demand.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 9

mustKnow.fact: A venous to arterial PCO2 gap above 6 mmHg means blood flow is low even when venous oxygen saturation looks acceptable.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 9

mustKnow.fact: Type A lactic acidosis is hypoperfusion. Type B lactic acidosis occurs with adrenaline, metformin, liver failure, or malignancy, so a high lactate is not proof of low flow.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 32

mustKnow.fact: The default ICU red cell transfusion threshold is a haemoglobin of 7 g/dL. TRICC and TRISS found a restrictive strategy as safe as a liberal strategy in the patients they enrolled.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 12

mustKnow.fact: Acute coronary syndrome is the setting where a higher transfusion threshold is still debated. The MINT trial did not show that a restrictive strategy was better than a liberal strategy.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 12

mustKnow.fact: Dysoxia means the cell cannot use delivered oxygen, as in cyanide poisoning. Venous saturation stays high while lactate rises, and more oxygen delivery does not correct it.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 9

topics.title: Haemodynamic monitoring
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 8 The Pulmonary Artery Catheter; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Functional Hemodynamic Monitoring

mustKnow.fact: Central venous pressure does not predict fluid responsiveness. It is useful as a trend and as the site for a central venous blood gas, and the old early goal directed target of 8 to 12 mmHg is not a resuscitation endpoint.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Functional Hemodynamic Monitoring

mustKnow.fact: Arterial pressure waveforms are checked with a fast flush square wave test. Overshoot means the system is underdamped, and a slurred wave means it is overdamped.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 8

mustKnow.fact: A pulmonary artery catheter measures cardiac output by thermodilution and pulmonary artery occlusion pressure. Routine use does not improve outcomes, and the catheter can knot, rupture the artery, or cause arrhythmia.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 8

mustKnow.fact: Transpulmonary thermodilution, as in PiCCO, gives extravascular lung water and a volumetric preload index. An extravascular lung water index above 10 mL/kg indicates pulmonary oedema.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Alternative Hemodynamic Monitoring

mustKnow.fact: Pulse pressure variation above 13% suggests fluid responsiveness only during fully controlled ventilation, sinus rhythm, a tidal volume of at least 8 mL/kg, and a closed chest. Spontaneous breathing invalidates it.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Functional Hemodynamic Monitoring

mustKnow.fact: A passive leg raise moves about 250 to 300 mL of blood into the chest and is reversed by putting the legs down. A rise in cardiac output of at least 10% predicts fluid responsiveness. A blood pressure rise alone is not enough.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Functional Hemodynamic Monitoring

mustKnow.fact: Pulse contour cardiac output drifts when vascular tone changes, so it is recalibrated after a large change in vasopressor dose.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Alternative Hemodynamic Monitoring

mustKnow.fact: An end expiratory occlusion of about 15 seconds can be used as a reversible fluid challenge in a passive patient. A rise in cardiac output predicts that a fluid bolus will raise output.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Functional Hemodynamic Monitoring

modules.name: Point of care ultrasound and echocardiography

topics.title: Point of care ultrasound and echocardiography
topics.book: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Basic Critical Care Ultrasound

mustKnow.fact: The BLUE protocol uses lung sliding and artefacts. Bilateral A lines with sliding suggest bronchospasm or embolism as the cause of dyspnoea, and bilateral anterior B lines suggest pulmonary oedema.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Basic Critical Care Ultrasound

mustKnow.fact: Lung sliding rules out pneumothorax at that interspace. Absent sliding with A lines is not enough. A lung point, where sliding reappears, confirms pneumothorax.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Basic Critical Care Ultrasound

mustKnow.fact: The RUSH exam looks at the pump, the tank, and the pipes: ventricular squeeze and pericardium, the inferior vena cava and free fluid, and the aorta and femoral veins.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Basic Critical Care Ultrasound

mustKnow.fact: In a spontaneously breathing patient, inferior vena cava collapse of more than 50% with a sniff suggests low right atrial pressure. It does not by itself prove that a fluid bolus will raise cardiac output.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Basic Critical Care Ultrasound

mustKnow.fact: In fully controlled ventilation, inferior vena cava distensibility above 18% is the cutoff often used to predict fluid responsiveness.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Basic Critical Care Ultrasound

mustKnow.fact: Tamponade is a clinical and Doppler diagnosis, not a fluid size. Right atrial systolic collapse, right ventricular diastolic collapse, and a plethoric inferior vena cava support it.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Basic Critical Care Ultrasound

mustKnow.fact: Stroke volume is left ventricular outflow tract velocity time integral times the cross sectional area. An integral around 18 to 22 cm is typical, and a rise of at least 10% with a passive leg raise predicts fluid responsiveness.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Basic Critical Care Ultrasound

mustKnow.fact: The extended FAST exam adds the pleural spaces to the perihepatic, perisplenic, pelvic, and pericardial views. A free fluid stripe in a shocked trauma patient is an indication to go to haemorrhage control, not to wait for a CT.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Basic Critical Care Ultrasound

topics.title: Respiratory mechanics and capnography
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 7 Oximetry and Capnography; Chang, Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation 4e Ch. 1

mustKnow.fact: Plateau pressure is measured with an end inspiratory hold when flow is zero. Peak pressure includes airway resistance. A high peak with a normal plateau is resistance, as in asthma. Both high means low compliance.
mustKnow.source: Chang, Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation 4e Ch. 1

mustKnow.fact: Driving pressure is plateau pressure minus total PEEP. In ARDS, a driving pressure above 15 cmH2O is associated with higher mortality. It is not itself a randomised target.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24

mustKnow.fact: Respiratory system compliance is tidal volume divided by plateau pressure minus total PEEP. Total PEEP includes auto-PEEP measured with an expiratory hold in a passive patient.
mustKnow.source: Chang, Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation 4e Ch. 1

mustKnow.fact: A time capnogram has a dead space phase, a transition, and an alveolar plateau. A slanted plateau means obstructed emptying. A sudden fall in end tidal CO2 means a fall in pulmonary blood flow, a disconnection, or oesophageal intubation.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 7

mustKnow.fact: Transpulmonary pressure is airway pressure minus pleural pressure, estimated with an oesophageal balloon. The EPVent-2 trial did not show a benefit of oesophageal pressure guided PEEP over an empiric high PEEP table.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24

mustKnow.fact: P0.1 is the airway pressure drop in the first 100 ms of an occluded breath. A P0.1 above about 3.5 cmH2O means respiratory drive is high.
mustKnow.source: Chang, Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation 4e Ch. 1

mustKnow.fact: On a constant flow breath, a stress index below 1 suggests tidal recruitment and a stress index above 1 suggests overdistension. An index near 1 is the shape associated with a safer tidal breath.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 27

mustKnow.fact: Electrical impedance tomography maps regional ventilation. It is a research and specialist tool, not a substitute for plateau pressure and driving pressure.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 27

topics.title: Neuromonitoring
topics.book: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Traumatic Brain Injury and Elevated Intracranial Pressure

mustKnow.fact: An external ventricular drain both measures intracranial pressure and drains cerebrospinal fluid. It is zeroed at the external auditory meatus, the surface mark for the foramen of Monro. An intraparenchymal monitor cannot drain.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Traumatic Brain Injury and Elevated Intracranial Pressure

mustKnow.fact: Cerebral perfusion pressure equals mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure. The Brain Trauma Foundation target range is 60 to 70 mmHg. Raising the pressure far above that does not improve outcome and can increase oedema.
mustKnow.source: Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines, 4th edition, 2016

mustKnow.fact: The Brain Trauma Foundation recommends treating intracranial pressure above 22 mmHg. A single high number is interpreted with the scan and the examination, not in isolation.
mustKnow.source: Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines, 4th edition, 2016

mustKnow.fact: An optic nerve sheath diameter above 5 mm suggests raised intracranial pressure. The exact cutoff varies between studies, and the measurement does not replace an invasive monitor when one is indicated.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Traumatic Brain Injury and Elevated Intracranial Pressure

mustKnow.fact: Transcranial Doppler middle cerebral artery mean velocity above 120 cm/s with a Lindegaard ratio above 3 suggests vasospasm. Velocity above 200 cm/s with a ratio above 6 suggests severe vasospasm. Velocity alone can also rise with hyperaemia.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage

mustKnow.fact: Continuous EEG is used to find nonconvulsive seizures in unexplained coma after convulsive status, cardiac arrest, or a structural brain injury.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Status Epilepticus

mustKnow.fact: Brain tissue oxygen tension below 20 mmHg is a commonly used treatment threshold. It is an adjunct to intracranial pressure, not a reason to ignore a high pressure.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Traumatic Brain Injury and Elevated Intracranial Pressure

mustKnow.fact: Jugular venous saturation is normally about 55% to 75%. A fall below 50% means the brain is extracting more because delivery is low. A very high value means flow is excessive or the brain is not using oxygen.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Traumatic Brain Injury and Elevated Intracranial Pressure

topics.title: Severity scores and ICU outcomes
topics.book: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Common Equations and Rules of Thumb; Sepsis-3 definitions, 2016

mustKnow.fact: APACHE II uses the worst physiological values in the first 24 hours, plus age and chronic health. It estimates group mortality. It is not a reason to withdraw treatment from one patient.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Common Equations and Rules of Thumb

mustKnow.fact: The SOFA score gives 0 to 4 points in six organ systems. Sepsis-3 defines sepsis as infection plus an acute rise in SOFA of at least 2 points.
mustKnow.source: Sepsis-3 definitions, JAMA 2016

mustKnow.fact: qSOFA counts respiratory rate at least 22, systolic pressure at most 100 mmHg, and altered mentation. Two or more is a prompt to look for sepsis outside the ICU. It is not the definition of sepsis and its sensitivity is poor.
mustKnow.source: Sepsis-3 definitions, JAMA 2016

mustKnow.fact: The Glasgow coma scale adds eye, verbal, and motor responses to a maximum of 15. The motor score carries the most prognostic information. A score of 8 or less is a prompt to protect the airway, not an absolute intubation law.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Coma

mustKnow.fact: RASS runs from minus 5, unrousable, to plus 4, combative. Zero is alert and calm. A sedation target of 0 to minus 2 is light sedation.
mustKnow.source: PADIS guidelines, 2018

mustKnow.fact: CAM-ICU is positive when onset is acute or fluctuating, attention fails, and there is either disorganised thinking or an altered level of consciousness.
mustKnow.source: PADIS guidelines, 2018

mustKnow.fact: The standardised mortality ratio is observed deaths divided by deaths predicted by the model. A model can discriminate well and still be poorly calibrated.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Common Equations and Rules of Thumb

mustKnow.fact: Lead time bias appears when treatment starts before the ICU, so the first ICU score looks better than the real insult. Comparing ICUs by raw scores without calibration is misleading.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Common Equations and Rules of Thumb

topics.title: Airway management in the ICU
topics.book: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Endotracheal Intubation

mustKnow.fact: The physiologically difficult airway is hypotension, right ventricular failure, severe acidosis, or hypoxaemia. Induction and positive pressure ventilation reduce venous return, so the patient is resuscitated before the tube when time allows.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Endotracheal Intubation

mustKnow.fact: The DEVICE trial showed a higher first attempt success with video laryngoscopy than with direct laryngoscopy in critically ill adults. A bougie is used when the view is poor.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Endotracheal Intubation

mustKnow.fact: The PREOXI trial showed that non-invasive ventilation for preoxygenation reduced hypoxaemia compared with an oxygen mask. Apnoeic oxygenation with high flow nasal oxygen is added when it does not delay the tube.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Endotracheal Intubation

mustKnow.fact: Ketamine is useful when blood pressure is low or when bronchospasm is present. The old absolute ban in raised intracranial pressure is not supported. Etomidate inhibits 11 beta hydroxylase, so many clinicians avoid it in septic shock.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Endotracheal Intubation

mustKnow.fact: For rapid sequence intubation, rocuronium is given at 1.2 mg/kg. Immediate reversal needs sugammadex 16 mg/kg. Succinylcholine is avoided after burns, denervation, rhabdomyolysis, and when potassium is already high.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Endotracheal Intubation

mustKnow.fact: A failed intubation follows a difficult airway algorithm: call for help, oxygenate with a supraglottic airway, and move to front of neck access if oxygen cannot be maintained. Do not repeat the same failing look.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Endotracheal Intubation

mustKnow.fact: Waveform capnography confirms tracheal placement. A single colour change on a colorimetric device can be misleading. Absent sustained end tidal CO2 means the tube is not in the trachea or pulmonary blood flow has stopped.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 7

mustKnow.fact: After the tube, the stomach is decompressed, the cuff pressure is kept near 20 to 30 cmH2O, and a lung protective tidal volume is set at once rather than a large default volume.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 27

modules.name: Modes of mechanical ventilation and waveforms

topics.title: Modes of mechanical ventilation and waveforms
topics.book: Chang, Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation 4e Ch. 3 and Ch. 4; Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 27

mustKnow.fact: Volume control sets tidal volume and flow, and airway pressure varies with compliance and resistance. Pressure control sets inspiratory pressure and time, and tidal volume falls when the lung stiffens.
mustKnow.source: Chang, Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation 4e Ch. 3

mustKnow.fact: Pressure support is a spontaneous mode. The patient triggers and the breath cycles when inspiratory flow falls to a set fraction of peak flow. There is no guaranteed rate unless backup apnoea ventilation is on.
mustKnow.source: Chang, Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation 4e Ch. 4

mustKnow.fact: SIMV interposes mandatory breaths with spontaneous breaths. It is not a weaning mode. The added work of breathing on the spontaneous breaths delays liberation.
mustKnow.source: Chang, Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation 4e Ch. 4

mustKnow.fact: PRVC, or pressure regulated volume control, targets a tidal volume by adjusting inspiratory pressure from breath to breath. It is still a pressure breath, and a sudden cough can make the ventilator drop the pressure and underdeliver.
mustKnow.source: Chang, Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation 4e Ch. 4

mustKnow.fact: APRV uses a long high pressure time and a short release. The short release generates auto-PEEP. It is not first line ARDS ventilation.
mustKnow.source: Chang, Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation 4e Ch. 4

mustKnow.fact: NAVA assists in proportion to the diaphragmatic electrical signal. Proportional assist ventilation assists in proportion to measured effort. Both need a reliable signal and an awake drive.
mustKnow.source: Chang, Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation 4e Ch. 4

mustKnow.fact: Double triggering stacks two breaths and raises tidal volume. Reverse triggering is diaphragmatic effort provoked by the ventilator breath, often under deep sedation, and it also stacks volume.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 27

mustKnow.fact: On a volume breath the flow waveform is set by the clinician, often a square wave. On a pressure breath the flow waveform is decelerating. Reading the wrong waveform leads to the wrong diagnosis of dyssynchrony.
mustKnow.source: Chang, Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation 4e Ch. 3

topics.title: Lung-protective ventilation and VILI
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24 Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome and Ch. 27 Conventional Mechanical Ventilation

mustKnow.fact: ARDSNet ARMA compared 6 mL/kg predicted body weight with 12 mL/kg and a plateau pressure limit of 30 cmH2O. The lower volume reduced mortality. The volume is predicted body weight, not actual weight.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24

mustKnow.fact: Predicted body weight in kilograms is 50 plus 0.91 times height in cm minus 152.4 for men, and 45.5 plus 0.91 times height in cm minus 152.4 for women.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24

mustKnow.fact: Volutrauma is overdistension, barotrauma is high transpulmonary pressure with air leak, atelectrauma is repeated opening and closing, and biotrauma is mediator release from those injuries.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24

mustKnow.fact: The ARDSNet lower PEEP FiO2 table was the table used in ARMA. Later trials of a higher PEEP table, including ALVEOLI, did not show a mortality benefit in unselected ARDS.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24

mustKnow.fact: The ART trial of a lung recruitment manoeuvre plus PEEP titration increased mortality. Routine recruitment manoeuvres are not used.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24

mustKnow.fact: Permissive hypercapnia is accepted to keep tidal volume and plateau pressure safe. In ARDSNet the pH was allowed to fall to 7.15, and bicarbonate was permitted below that.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24

mustKnow.fact: Mechanical power combines tidal volume, pressure, flow, and rate. Higher power is associated with worse outcomes. There is no single mandated safe cutoff to put on a ventilator order.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 27

mustKnow.fact: Driving pressure above 15 cmH2O tracks mortality in observational ARDS data. Limiting it means lowering tidal volume or raising PEEP only when that does not raise plateau pressure unsafely.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24

modules.name: Non-invasive ventilation and high flow nasal oxygen

topics.title: Non-invasive ventilation and high flow nasal oxygen
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 25 Oxygen Inhalation and Ch. 26 Noninvasive Ventilation; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Noninvasive Ventilation

mustKnow.fact: In FLORALI, high flow nasal oxygen did not clearly cut intubation in the whole group, but 90 day mortality was lower than with non-invasive ventilation or standard oxygen in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 26

mustKnow.fact: The ROX index is SpO2 over FiO2, divided by respiratory rate. A value below 3.85 at 12 hours predicts high flow failure. A value above 4.88 suggests success.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 26

mustKnow.fact: Non-invasive ventilation is first line for a COPD exacerbation with respiratory acidosis when the pH is about 7.25 to 7.35, and for cardiogenic pulmonary oedema treated with CPAP.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Noninvasive Ventilation

mustKnow.fact: Helmet non-invasive ventilation can deliver prolonged pressure support with less skin breakdown than a face mask. It still needs a clear plan for intubation if work of breathing stays high.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Noninvasive Ventilation

mustKnow.fact: Patient self inflicted lung injury is vigorous spontaneous breathing that overdistends and swings pleural pressure. It is a reason to intubate or deepen sedation, not to watch a tiring patient on high flow.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 26

mustKnow.fact: After extubation, high flow or non-invasive ventilation prevents reintubation in high risk patients, including those with hypercapnia or heart failure. Routine non-invasive ventilation in low risk patients can delay a needed reintubation.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Weaning of Mechanical Ventilation

mustKnow.fact: The HACOR score combines heart rate, acidosis, consciousness, oxygenation, and respiratory rate to flag non-invasive ventilation failure. A rising score is a prompt to intubate.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Noninvasive Ventilation

mustKnow.fact: Awake prone positioning improves oxygenation in hypoxaemic patients who are not intubated. It is not a substitute for intubation when work of breathing is unsustainable.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, COVID-19 and Other Viral Pneumonias

topics.title: Weaning and liberation from ventilation
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 30 Discontinuing Mechanical Ventilation; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Weaning of Mechanical Ventilation

mustKnow.fact: A spontaneous breathing trial lasts 30 to 120 minutes on a T piece or on pressure support of about 5 to 8 cmH2O with PEEP 5. Failure is distress, rising PaCO2, hypoxia, or haemodynamic instability.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 30

mustKnow.fact: The rapid shallow breathing index is respiratory rate divided by tidal volume in litres, measured over a minute on a T piece. A value below 105 favours extubation and does not by itself authorise it.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 30

mustKnow.fact: The Awakening and Breathing Controlled trial showed that pairing a spontaneous awakening trial with a breathing trial reduced time on the ventilator and reduced mortality compared with usual sedation practice.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 6 and Ch. 30

mustKnow.fact: An absent cuff leak, often a volume difference below 110 mL, predicts post extubation stridor. A short course of corticosteroid before extubation is reasonable in that high risk patient.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 30

mustKnow.fact: The TracMan trial compared tracheostomy within 4 days with tracheostomy after day 10. Early tracheostomy did not reduce mortality.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 30

mustKnow.fact: The ABCDEF bundle is awakening, breathing coordination, delirium monitoring, early mobility, and family engagement. It is a daily checklist, not a single drug.
mustKnow.source: PADIS guidelines, 2018

mustKnow.fact: Extubation failure means reintubation within about 48 hours. Non-invasive ventilation can rescue a hypercapnic COPD patient. It should not be used to delay reintubation in a patient who has failed with hypoxaemic distress.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Weaning of Mechanical Ventilation

mustKnow.fact: A diaphragm thickening fraction below about 30% on ultrasound is associated with weaning failure. It does not replace a breathing trial.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Weaning of Mechanical Ventilation

topics.title: Ventilation in obstructive airway disease
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 23 Asthma and COPD in the ICU; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Severe Asthma

mustKnow.fact: Dynamic hyperinflation in asthma and COPD is treated with a low respiratory rate, a long expiratory time, and a tidal volume near 6 to 8 mL/kg. Minute ventilation is limited on purpose.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 23

mustKnow.fact: Sudden hypotension on the ventilator in asthma is often auto-PEEP impairing venous return. Disconnect the circuit and let the chest empty, then give fluid. Do not start by raising the rate.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 23

mustKnow.fact: External PEEP in triggered COPD is set below measured auto-PEEP, often near 80% of it, to reduce the effort needed to trigger. In a paralysed asthmatic patient, external PEEP is not routinely stacked on top of auto-PEEP.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 23

mustKnow.fact: Permissive hypercapnia is accepted in status asthmaticus. A high plateau pressure is a signal to lower minute ventilation, not to add more breaths.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Severe Asthma

mustKnow.fact: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g is an adjunct in acute severe asthma that is not responding. It is not a substitute for oxygen, nebulised bronchodilators, and corticosteroids.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Severe Asthma

mustKnow.fact: Ketamine is a bronchodilator and an induction option in status asthmaticus. Heliox with at least 70% helium reduces turbulent flow when oxygen needs allow that mix.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Severe Asthma

mustKnow.fact: For a COPD exacerbation, non-invasive ventilation is started when there is respiratory acidosis, and invasive ventilation uses the same long expiratory time. Oxygen is targeted, not left at a high uncontrolled FiO2.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Exacerbations of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease

mustKnow.fact: A pneumothorax in obstructed ventilation can be tension physiology from gas trapping as well as from a ruptured alveolus. Falling blood pressure with rising peak pressure prompts disconnection and a search for pneumothorax.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 23

topics.title: Oxygen therapy and targets
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 25 Oxygen Inhalation

mustKnow.fact: ICU-ROX compared a conservative oxygen saturation target with usual care and did not show a mortality benefit for the conservative arm.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 25

mustKnow.fact: HOT-ICU compared a PaO2 target near 60 mmHg with a target near 90 mmHg. Mortality was not different.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 25

mustKnow.fact: Hyperoxaemia causes absorption atelectasis and vasoconstriction. A saturation of 100% on a high FiO2 is a prompt to lower the FiO2, not a trophy.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 25

mustKnow.fact: A Venturi mask gives a known FiO2 if the flow is adequate. A non-rebreather reservoir mask is for high FiO2 and is not a precise oxygen prescription.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 25

mustKnow.fact: In a COPD exacerbation the oxygen target is about 88% to 92% until the blood gas is known, because uncontrolled oxygen can worsen hypercapnia.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Exacerbations of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease

mustKnow.fact: Hyperbaric oxygen shortens the half life of carboxyhaemoglobin and is considered for carbon monoxide poisoning with loss of consciousness, cardiac ischaemia, pregnancy, or a very high level. It is not first line for ordinary hypoxaemia.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 53

mustKnow.fact: Oxygen toxicity of the lung is a reason to lower FiO2 toward 0.6 or less once saturation allows. PEEP is adjusted so that the lower FiO2 still holds the saturation target.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 25

mustKnow.fact: A target saturation of 92% to 96% is a reasonable default for most critically ill adults when no tighter trial target is specified. The exceptions are carbon monoxide, pneumothorax on the way to drainage, and cluster headache, which are not ordinary ICU hypoxaemia.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 25

topics.title: ARDS definition and pathophysiology
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24 Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, The Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome

mustKnow.fact: The Berlin definition requires acute onset within 7 days, bilateral opacities not fully explained by effusion or collapse, and respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure, with PEEP at least 5 cmH2O.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24

mustKnow.fact: Berlin severity uses PaO2/FiO2 on at least 5 cmH2O PEEP: mild 200 to 300, moderate 100 to 200, and severe 100 or below.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24

mustKnow.fact: The 2023 global definition allows SpO2/FiO2 when an arterial gas is unavailable, and it allows the diagnosis on high flow nasal oxygen. It does not retire lung protective ventilation.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, The Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome

mustKnow.fact: The histological pattern of diffuse alveolar damage has an early exudative phase, then a proliferative phase, then fibrosis in those who do not resolve. Biopsy is not required to treat ARDS.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24

mustKnow.fact: A hyperinflammatory ARDS subphenotype has higher cytokines and higher mortality. Bedside treatment is not yet assigned by phenotype outside trials.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, The Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome

mustKnow.fact: ARDS is not cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. A high left atrial pressure can coexist, but the defining injury is increased alveolar capillary permeability.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24

mustKnow.fact: Common triggers are pneumonia, non-pulmonary sepsis, aspiration, and trauma. Identifying the trigger matters because the ventilator does not treat the cause.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, The Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome

mustKnow.fact: The PaO2/FiO2 ratio falls when PEEP is removed, so severity is quoted with the PEEP in use. A single ratio on a face mask is not a Berlin grade.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24

topics.title: ARDS management
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24 Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome

mustKnow.fact: PROSEVA used prone positioning for at least 16 hours a day in ARDS with PaO2/FiO2 below 150. It reduced mortality. Proning is started early, not after days of refractory hypoxia.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24

mustKnow.fact: ACURASYS found that 48 hours of cisatracurium in severe ARDS reduced mortality in an era of deep sedation. The ROSE trial, with lighter sedation, did not reproduce that benefit. Paralysis is reserved for ventilator dyssynchrony, not given to every patient.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24

mustKnow.fact: FACTT compared a conservative fluid strategy with a liberal strategy after shock had resolved. The conservative arm increased ventilator free days and did not change mortality.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24

mustKnow.fact: The DEXA-ARDS trial of dexamethasone in moderate to severe ARDS, before COVID-19, reduced ventilator time and mortality. It does not licence steroid for every mild postoperative hypoxaemia.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24

mustKnow.fact: Inhaled nitric oxide raises PaO2 for a time and does not reduce mortality. It is a bridge toward proning or ECMO, not a standard ARDS drug.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24

mustKnow.fact: Higher PEEP is considered when the PaO2/FiO2 is very low and the right ventricle tolerates it. A recruitment manoeuvre as used in the ART trial is not routine because mortality rose.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24

mustKnow.fact: Refractory hypoxaemia is managed in order: check the tube and the circuit, optimise PEEP and volume, prone, treat the driver, and refer for VV-ECMO if criteria are met. Do not raise tidal volume to chase saturation.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24

mustKnow.fact: Sedation for proning is enough to stop the patient pulling out tubes. Deep sedation and paralysis for days without a breathing trial causes weakness and is not the PROSEVA protocol.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 24

topics.title: Extracorporeal life support
topics.book: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Extracorporeal Life Support

mustKnow.fact: EOLIA enrolled very severe ARDS, including PaO2/FiO2 below 50 for more than 3 hours or below 80 for more than 6 hours despite optimisation. The primary 60 day mortality difference was not statistically significant, and many control patients crossed over to ECMO.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Extracorporeal Life Support

mustKnow.fact: CESAR randomised transfer to an ECMO centre, not ECMO itself. Survival without severe disability was better in the transfer arm. Not every transferred patient received ECMO.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Extracorporeal Life Support

mustKnow.fact: VV-ECMO supports gas exchange and does not provide cardiac output. VA-ECMO bypasses the heart and lungs and does provide flow. The configuration is chosen from the failing organ.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Extracorporeal Life Support

mustKnow.fact: Harlequin, or north south, syndrome on peripheral VA-ECMO occurs when the recovering heart ejects poorly oxygenated blood to the upper body while the femoral return oxygenates the legs. The right radial arterial gas detects it.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Extracorporeal Life Support

mustKnow.fact: Peripheral VA-ECMO increases left ventricular afterload. A distended, non-ejecting left ventricle needs a vent, such as an Impella, a septostomy, or an intra-aortic balloon.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Extracorporeal Life Support

mustKnow.fact: Circuit anticoagulation is usually unfractionated heparin, monitored by anti-Xa or ACT. Bleeding, not clotting alone, is the complication that most often limits support.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Extracorporeal Life Support

mustKnow.fact: The RESP score estimates survival on respiratory ECMO. The SAVE score estimates survival on cardiac ECMO. Both are counselling tools, not a refusal rule used alone.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Extracorporeal Life Support

mustKnow.fact: Extracorporeal carbon dioxide removal uses low blood flow and does not oxygenate. It is not standard ARDS care. ECPR is VA-ECMO started during cardiac arrest, and it is limited to systems that can cannulate without a long no-flow time.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Extracorporeal Life Support

modules.name: Acute hypoxaemic and hypercapnic respiratory failure

topics.title: Acute hypoxaemic and hypercapnic respiratory failure
topics.book: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, An Approach to Respiratory Failure; Chang, Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation 4e Ch. 1

mustKnow.fact: Hypoxaemia has five mechanisms: low inspired oxygen, hypoventilation, diffusion limitation, ventilation perfusion mismatch, and shunt. Shunt does not correct fully with added oxygen.
mustKnow.source: Chang, Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation 4e Ch. 1

mustKnow.fact: The alveolar to arterial oxygen gradient is high in mismatch, shunt, and diffusion limitation. It is normal in hypoventilation and low inspired oxygen, which separates those causes.
mustKnow.source: Chang, Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation 4e Ch. 1

mustKnow.fact: Hypercapnic failure is ventilatory pump failure: low drive, weakness, or a load the patient cannot meet, as in severe airway obstruction. Hypoxaemic failure is lung parenchymal failure.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, An Approach to Respiratory Failure

mustKnow.fact: A COPD exacerbation with acidosis is treated first with non-invasive ventilation, controlled oxygen, bronchodilators, and steroids. Intubation is for exhaustion, vomiting, or a falling pH despite non-invasive ventilation.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Exacerbations of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease

mustKnow.fact: Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema responds to CPAP or non-invasive ventilation plus treatment of the heart. It is not treated as ARDS with a dry strategy until the filling pressure is addressed.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Decompensated Heart Failure

mustKnow.fact: Neuromuscular respiratory failure, as in Guillain-Barre syndrome or myasthenic crisis, shows a falling vital capacity and weak cough before the gas is severely abnormal. Waiting for hypercapnia is late.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Neuromuscular Disorders in the Critically Ill

mustKnow.fact: The 20, 30, 40 rule is a teaching trigger for intubation in neuromuscular weakness: vital capacity below 20 mL/kg, maximum inspiratory pressure worse than minus 30 cmH2O, or maximum expiratory pressure below 40 cmH2O.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Neuromuscular Disorders in the Critically Ill

mustKnow.fact: Type 1 and type 2 respiratory failure can coexist. The first blood gas and the examination decide whether the patient needs oxygen, pressure support, or a protected airway.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, An Approach to Respiratory Failure

topics.title: Severe pneumonia and VAP
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 29 Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Community-Acquired Pneumonia and Nosocomial Pneumonia

mustKnow.fact: IDSA/ATS severe community acquired pneumonia is one major criterion, invasive ventilation or septic shock, or three minor criteria. That severity is what selects the ICU and broader antibiotics.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Community-Acquired Pneumonia

mustKnow.fact: CAPE COD showed that hydrocortisone reduced 28 day mortality in severe community acquired pneumonia in the ICU. It is not a steroid prescription for every ward pneumonia.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Community-Acquired Pneumonia

mustKnow.fact: Ventilator associated pneumonia is suspected from a new infiltrate plus fever, purulent sputum, or worsening gas exchange. The Clinical Pulmonary Infection Score is not accurate enough to use alone.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 29

mustKnow.fact: IDSA 2016 suggests non-invasive sampling, such as an endotracheal aspirate, rather than insisting on a bronchoalveolar lavage for every patient. Quantitative cultures are an option, not a requirement.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 29

mustKnow.fact: A 7 day antibiotic course is enough for most ventilator associated pneumonia that is responding. Longer courses are for Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, or a slow clinical response, not for every case.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 29

mustKnow.fact: Prevention is head of bed elevation, daily sedation breaks, and subglottic secretion drainage. Routine circuit changes do not prevent pneumonia. Oral chlorhexidine is no longer assumed to be harmless.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 29

mustKnow.fact: Empiric cover follows local resistance and risk of methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas. Double gram negative cover is stopped once susceptibilities return.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Nosocomial Pneumonia

mustKnow.fact: A parapneumonic effusion that is frankly purulent, culture positive, or pH below 7.20 is drained. Antibiotics alone do not treat an empyema.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Pleural Disorders in the Intensive Care Unit

modules.name: Viral pneumonia and pandemic critical care

topics.title: Viral pneumonia and pandemic critical care
topics.book: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, COVID-19 and Other Viral Pneumonias

mustKnow.fact: RECOVERY showed that dexamethasone 6 mg daily for up to 10 days reduced 28 day mortality in COVID-19 patients who needed oxygen or ventilation. Patients who did not need oxygen were not helped.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, COVID-19 and Other Viral Pneumonias

mustKnow.fact: REMAP-CAP found that tocilizumab improved outcomes in critically ill COVID-19. Baricitinib is an alternative immunomodulator in patients with progressing disease and inflammation.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, COVID-19 and Other Viral Pneumonias

mustKnow.fact: COVID-19 ARDS is still ARDS for the ventilator: 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, plateau pressure at most 30 cmH2O, and prone positioning when the PaO2/FiO2 is below 150.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, COVID-19 and Other Viral Pneumonias

mustKnow.fact: Awake prone positioning is used in hypoxaemic COVID-19 before intubation. It does not replace intubation when the work of breathing is rising.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, COVID-19 and Other Viral Pneumonias

mustKnow.fact: Oseltamivir is given for severe influenza even when symptom onset was more than 48 hours earlier. Antibiotics are added only when bacterial coinfection is likely, not as a reflex.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, COVID-19 and Other Viral Pneumonias

mustKnow.fact: Routine antibacterial therapy and routine therapeutic anticoagulation are not treatments for viral pneumonia. Prophylactic anticoagulation still applies unless bleeding forbids it.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, COVID-19 and Other Viral Pneumonias

mustKnow.fact: Surge triage uses a published framework and a physiology score such as SOFA. It does not use social worth. The same rules apply to every patient when crisis standards are declared.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, COVID-19 and Other Viral Pneumonias

mustKnow.fact: Staff protection is fit tested respiratory protection for aerosol generating procedures, including intubation. A viral pandemic plan names the device, the team, and the doffing area before the patient arrives.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, COVID-19 and Other Viral Pneumonias

topics.title: Approach to shock
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 14 Approaches to Clinical Shock; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Introduction to Shock

mustKnow.fact: Shock is inadequate tissue perfusion. The four bedside patterns are hypovolaemic, distributive, cardiogenic, and obstructive. Ultrasound and the examination sort them before a long fluid trial.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Introduction to Shock

mustKnow.fact: The shock index is heart rate divided by systolic pressure. A value above 1 suggests significant blood loss or shock and is more sensitive than blood pressure alone.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Introduction to Shock

mustKnow.fact: The initial mean arterial pressure target in septic and vasodilatory shock is 65 mmHg. The 65 trial and SEPSISPAM did not show an overall mortality benefit from a higher default target.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 17

mustKnow.fact: SEPSISPAM suggested that a higher mean pressure, near 80 to 85 mmHg, reduced the need for renal replacement in patients with chronic hypertension, at the cost of more atrial fibrillation. It is not the starting target for everyone.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 17

mustKnow.fact: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK compared capillary refill guided resuscitation with lactate guided resuscitation. The mortality difference was not statistically significant. Capillary refill longer than 3 seconds is still a useful perfusion sign.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Introduction to Shock

mustKnow.fact: Lactate clearance reassures, but chasing a normal lactate with more fluid after perfusion has recovered causes overload. Type B lactate will not clear with fluid.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 14

mustKnow.fact: A low mixed venous saturation with a high lactate suggests delivery failure. A high mixed venous saturation with a high lactate suggests distributive shock or a utilisation defect.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 14

mustKnow.fact: The first hour is for the cause: bleeding control, a drain for tamponade, a needle for tension pneumothorax, antibiotics and source control for sepsis, and reperfusion for cardiogenic shock. Vasopressors do not replace that.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Introduction to Shock

topics.title: Fluid therapy and resuscitation
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 10 Intravenous Fluids and Ch. 11 Fluid Management

mustKnow.fact: SMART found that balanced crystalloid reduced the composite of death, new renal replacement, and persistent renal dysfunction compared with saline in critically ill adults.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 10

mustKnow.fact: PLUS and BaSICS did not show a 90 day mortality difference between a balanced solution and saline. Saline still causes a hyperchloremic acidosis when large volumes are used.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 10

mustKnow.fact: The SAFE trial found no overall mortality difference between 4% albumin and saline. Albumin was associated with harm in traumatic brain injury, so it is avoided there.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 10

mustKnow.fact: The 6S trial found that hydroxyethyl starch increased 90 day mortality in sepsis. CHEST found that starch increased the need for renal replacement. Starch is not used.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 10

mustKnow.fact: ALBIOS found no mortality benefit of albumin in severe sepsis. Surviving Sepsis suggests albumin only when large volumes of crystalloid have already been given, as a weak suggestion.
mustKnow.source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021

mustKnow.fact: CLASSIC tested restriction of fluid after the initial resuscitation of septic shock and found no mortality difference. CLOVERS found no difference between a restrictive and a liberal early fluid strategy.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 11

mustKnow.fact: Surviving Sepsis still suggests at least 30 mL/kg of crystalloid for sepsis induced hypoperfusion or a lactate of at least 4 mmol/L, then an assessment of further fluid rather than an automatic second bolus.
mustKnow.source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021

mustKnow.fact: De-resuscitation starts when the patient is no longer fluid responsive and oedema is harming ventilation or the abdomen. A diuretic or ultrafiltration removes fluid. More crystalloid does not.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 11

topics.title: Vasopressors and inotropes
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 17 Inflammatory Shock Syndromes; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021

mustKnow.fact: Noradrenaline is the first line vasopressor in septic shock. Adrenaline is added, or substituted, when noradrenaline does not restore perfusion. Dopamine is not first line because it causes more arrhythmia.
mustKnow.source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021

mustKnow.fact: VASST found no overall mortality difference between vasopressin and noradrenaline. Vasopressin is a second agent to raise mean pressure or to reduce the noradrenaline dose, typically at a fixed 0.03 units per minute. It is not titrated like noradrenaline.
mustKnow.source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021

mustKnow.fact: ATHOS-3 showed that angiotensin II increased the proportion of patients with refractory vasodilatory shock who met a mean pressure target at 3 hours. It is a rescue drug, not a first line drug.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 17

mustKnow.fact: Dobutamine is the inotrope for persistent hypoperfusion with cardiac dysfunction after volume and pressure are adequate. Levosimendan did not improve outcomes in LeoPARDS and is not routine.
mustKnow.source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021

mustKnow.fact: Phenylephrine is a pure alpha agonist used when tachyarrhythmia forbids noradrenaline. It can drop cardiac output by raising afterload, so it is a poor choice in a failing left ventricle.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 17

mustKnow.fact: Milrinone is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor that dilates the pulmonary vascular bed and can worsen hypotension. It is an option in right ventricular failure when blood pressure allows, not a reflex inotrope.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 16

mustKnow.fact: Methylene blue inhibits the nitric oxide pathway and is a rescue for refractory vasoplegia. It is avoided in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency and with serotonergic drugs.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 17

mustKnow.fact: A peripheral vasopressor is acceptable for a short time if central access would delay treatment, with a protocol for extravasation. Phentolamine is the local antidote for a tissue injury from extravasation.
mustKnow.source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021

modules.name: Cardiogenic shock and mechanical circulatory support

topics.title: Cardiogenic shock and mechanical circulatory support
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 16 Cardiogenic Shock and Ch. 18 Acute Heart Failure; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Cardiogenic Shock

mustKnow.fact: SCAI shock stages run from A, at risk, to E, extremis. The stage is reassessed after each intervention because a patient moves between stages in hours.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Cardiogenic Shock

mustKnow.fact: In infarct related cardiogenic shock with multivessel disease, CULPRIT-SHOCK showed that culprit lesion only PCI, with later staged revascularisation, was better than immediate multivessel PCI.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 20

mustKnow.fact: IABP-SHOCK II found that a routine intra-aortic balloon pump did not reduce 30 day mortality in infarct related cardiogenic shock. A balloon is not inserted by default.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 16

mustKnow.fact: DanGer Shock found that Impella CP reduced 180 day death in selected patients with ST elevation myocardial infarction and cardiogenic shock. That result does not extend to every non-ischaemic shock.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Cardiogenic Shock

mustKnow.fact: ECLS-SHOCK found that early VA-ECMO did not reduce 30 day death in infarct related cardiogenic shock. ECMO is not the default mechanical support.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Extracorporeal Life Support

mustKnow.fact: Right ventricular infarction presents with hypotension, clear lungs, and a raised jugular venous pressure. Treatment is reperfusion, cautious fluid, and avoidance of nitrates. A pulmonary artery catheter shows a high right pressure and a low or normal wedge.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 16

mustKnow.fact: The cold and wet profile is low cardiac output with pulmonary congestion and is the classic cardiogenic shock bed. Cold and dry is low output without congestion. Warm and wet is congestion with a preserved output.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 18

mustKnow.fact: Noradrenaline is preferred to dopamine when a vasopressor is needed in cardiogenic shock. Dobutamine is added for low output once the pressure is high enough for coronary perfusion.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Cardiogenic Shock

modules.name: Obstructive shock and massive pulmonary embolism

topics.title: Obstructive shock and massive pulmonary embolism
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 22 Acute Pulmonary Embolism; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Mechanical Causes of Shock

mustKnow.fact: Cardiac tamponade equalises diastolic pressures. Pulsus paradoxus, a plethoric inferior vena cava, and chamber collapse on echo support the diagnosis. Electrical alternans is a late ECG clue. The treatment is drainage, not fluid alone.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Mechanical Causes of Shock

mustKnow.fact: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis in a crashing patient: absent breath sounds, tracheal shift, and hypotension. Decompress, then place a chest drain. Do not wait for a chest radiograph.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Mechanical Causes of Shock

mustKnow.fact: Massive pulmonary embolism is embolism with hypotension. Systemic thrombolysis is alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours if bleeding risk allows. Cardiac arrest from suspected embolism may be treated with a 50 mg bolus while resuscitation continues.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 22

mustKnow.fact: Catheter directed therapy is for massive or high intermediate embolism when systemic thrombolysis is contraindicated or has failed, in a centre that can do it. It is not the first step in a stable patient.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 22

mustKnow.fact: McConnell sign, apical sparing of the right ventricle, is not specific for embolism. A dilated right ventricle in shock has a differential of embolism, right ventricular infarct, and pulmonary hypertension.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 22

mustKnow.fact: Intermediate risk embolism has right ventricular strain or a positive troponin or BNP without hypotension. Thrombolysis is not routine in that group. Rescue thrombolysis is for deterioration.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Pulmonary Embolism

mustKnow.fact: Acute right ventricular failure is worsened by high airway pressure, acidosis, and hypoxia, all of which raise pulmonary vascular resistance. Noradrenaline supports perfusion pressure. Fluid is given only if the ventricle is underfilled.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Pulmonary Hypertension and Right Ventricular Failure

mustKnow.fact: Abdominal compartment syndrome can obstruct venous return and mimic obstructive shock. A bladder pressure above 20 mmHg with new organ failure defines it, and refractory cases need decompression.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, The Acute Abdomen

topics.title: Haemorrhagic shock and massive transfusion
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 15 Hemorrhagic Shock

mustKnow.fact: Damage control resuscitation is early blood products, limited crystalloid, permissive hypotension until bleeding is controlled, and rapid surgery or angioembolisation. It does not apply unchanged to traumatic brain injury.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 15

mustKnow.fact: PROPPR compared a 1:1:1 ratio of plasma, platelets, and red cells with 1:1:2. More patients achieved haemostasis with 1:1:1. Mortality at 24 hours and 30 days was not significantly different.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 15

mustKnow.fact: CRASH-2 showed that tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours, reduced death from bleeding when given within 3 hours of injury. Giving it after 3 hours was associated with harm.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 15

mustKnow.fact: Permissive hypotension targets a systolic pressure around 80 to 90 mmHg until surgical control, and only if there is no traumatic brain injury. With brain injury the pressure is kept higher, commonly a systolic pressure of at least 110 mmHg.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 15

mustKnow.fact: Viscoelastic tests, TEG or ROTEM, guide product replacement when they are available. A low fibrinogen, below about 150 to 200 mg/dL, is replaced with cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 15

mustKnow.fact: Citrate in blood products binds calcium. Ionised calcium is checked and replaced during massive transfusion. Hypocalcaemia worsens coagulopathy and cardiac function.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 15

mustKnow.fact: Prothrombin complex concentrate reverses warfarin faster than plasma and with less volume. It does not replace fibrinogen and it does not reverse a platelet problem.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 13

mustKnow.fact: Crystalloid resuscitation of haemorrhage dilutes clotting factors and does not carry oxygen. It is a bridge only until blood arrives.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 15

modules.name: Arrhythmias and acute cardiac care in the ICU

topics.title: Arrhythmias and acute cardiac care in the ICU
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 19 Tachyarrhythmias and Ch. 20 Acute Coronary Syndromes; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Cardiac Arrhythmias

mustKnow.fact: New atrial fibrillation in the ICU is often secondary to sepsis, withdrawal, or atrial stretch. Unstable patients are electrically cardioverted. Stable patients are rate controlled, and anticoagulation depends on stroke risk and bleeding risk, not on a reflex heparin infusion.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Cardiac Arrhythmias and Conduction Abnormalities

mustKnow.fact: Amiodarone is the usual rhythm drug when structural heart disease is present. It causes hypotension when infused fast, and long term use causes thyroid and lung toxicity that outlasts the ICU stay.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 19

mustKnow.fact: Synchronised cardioversion is for unstable tachyarrhythmias with a pulse. Pulseless ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation are defibrillated, not synchronised.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 19

mustKnow.fact: Torsades de pointes is treated with magnesium sulfate 2 g even when the serum magnesium is normal, with correction of potassium, and with pacing or isoproterenol if the rhythm is pause dependent. The offending QT drug is stopped.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 19

mustKnow.fact: Transvenous pacing is for symptomatic bradycardia that does not respond to atropine or chronotropic infusion, and for overdrive pacing of recurrent pause dependent torsades. Asynchronous pacing on a T wave can induce ventricular fibrillation.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Cardiac Arrhythmias and Conduction Abnormalities

mustKnow.fact: Acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary oedema is treated with non-invasive ventilation, a nitrate if the pressure allows, and a diuretic. Inotropes are for low output shock, not for every wet patient.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Decompensated Heart Failure

mustKnow.fact: A hypertensive emergency is organ injury, not a number alone: encephalopathy, pulmonary oedema, acute coronary syndrome, dissection, or eclampsia. The pressure is lowered in a controlled way, not normalised in minutes, except in aortic dissection and eclampsia where the fall is faster.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Approach to Hypertensive Emergencies

mustKnow.fact: ST elevation myocardial infarction in the ICU still goes to immediate reperfusion. A new murmur after infarction suggests mechanical complication: ventricular septal rupture, papillary muscle rupture, or free wall rupture.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 20

modules.name: Cardiac arrest and post resuscitation care

topics.title: Cardiac arrest and post resuscitation care
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 21 Cardiac Arrest; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Post-Cardiac Arrest Management

mustKnow.fact: High quality CPR is a rate of 100 to 120 per minute, a depth of 5 to 6 cm, full chest recoil, and minimal pauses. With an advanced airway, ventilation is 10 breaths per minute so that ventilation does not interrupt compressions.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 21

mustKnow.fact: Shockable rhythms are ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Asystole and pulseless electrical activity are not shocked. Adrenaline is given as soon as vascular access exists in a non-shockable rhythm, and after the initial shocks in a shockable rhythm.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 21

mustKnow.fact: PARAMEDIC2 showed that adrenaline increased 30 day survival and did not increase favourable neurological survival. Amiodarone or lidocaine is used for refractory shockable rhythms. Neither replaces defibrillation.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 21

mustKnow.fact: Reversible causes are listed as the Hs and Ts: hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hydrogen ion, hypo or hyperkalaemia, hypothermia, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, and thrombosis of the coronary or pulmonary artery.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 21

mustKnow.fact: TTM2 compared hypothermia at 33 C with normothermia and early treatment of fever. Hypothermia did not improve outcome and caused more arrhythmia. Fever is prevented. Routine cooling to 33 C is not required.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Post-Cardiac Arrest Management

mustKnow.fact: After return of circulation, avoid hypoxia and hyperoxia, target normocapnia, and support a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mmHg. ST elevation or cardiogenic shock goes to coronary angiography.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Post-Cardiac Arrest Management

mustKnow.fact: Neuroprognostication is multimodal and is not done before 72 hours when sedation may still be present. No single sign, including one unreactive pupil on day 1, is used alone to withdraw care.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Post-Cardiac Arrest Management

mustKnow.fact: The useful later signs are absent pupillary and corneal reflexes, a highly malignant EEG, a high neuron specific enolase, and diffuse anoxic injury on imaging. Status myoclonus with a malignant EEG is ominous. Isolated myoclonus is not.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Post-Cardiac Arrest Management

sections.name: Sepsis and infection in the ICU

topics.title: Sepsis definitions and pathophysiology
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 17 Inflammatory Shock Syndromes; Sepsis-3 definitions, 2016

mustKnow.fact: Sepsis-3 defines sepsis as life threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response, recognised as infection plus an acute SOFA rise of at least 2 points. SIRS is not the definition.
mustKnow.source: Sepsis-3 definitions, JAMA 2016

mustKnow.fact: Septic shock is a vasopressor requirement to keep mean arterial pressure at least 65 mmHg plus a lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid. Either finding alone is not the definition.
mustKnow.source: Sepsis-3 definitions, JAMA 2016

mustKnow.fact: qSOFA is a bedside prompt outside the ICU, not a diagnostic criterion. A low qSOFA does not exclude sepsis.
mustKnow.source: Sepsis-3 definitions, JAMA 2016

mustKnow.fact: Endothelial glycocalyx injury increases permeability, so fluid leaves the vessels and the patient becomes oedematous while still intravascularly depleted early on.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 17

mustKnow.fact: Later sepsis includes immunoparalysis, with falling monocyte HLA-DR and secondary infection. More immunosuppression is not the treatment of that phase.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 17

mustKnow.fact: Sepsis induced coagulopathy is a distinct score from overt DIC. Thrombocytopenia and a rising INR in sepsis are a reason to look for DIC, not an automatic plasma transfusion.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 17

mustKnow.fact: A cytokine storm is the phenotype of some viral and CAR-T illnesses. Ordinary bacterial sepsis is not treated with cytokine blockade outside a specific indication such as COVID-19.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Sepsis and Septic Shock

mustKnow.fact: Mitochondrial dysfunction is one reason lactate stays high after perfusion has been restored. It is not fixed by another litre of fluid.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 17

topics.title: Sepsis resuscitation and management
topics.book: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 17

mustKnow.fact: For possible septic shock, or a high likelihood of sepsis, Surviving Sepsis recommends antibiotics immediately, ideally within 1 hour. When sepsis is possible but shock is absent, investigate rapidly and give antibiotics within 3 hours if concern persists.
mustKnow.source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021

mustKnow.fact: Blood cultures are taken before antibiotics when that does not delay the dose. Source control is done as soon as it is logistically possible. A clock does not postpone a needed operation.
mustKnow.source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021

mustKnow.fact: The hour-1 bundle includes lactate, cultures, antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypoperfusion or lactate at least 4 mmol/L, and a vasopressor if the patient is hypotensive during or after fluid.
mustKnow.source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021

mustKnow.fact: Rivers early goal directed therapy was not confirmed by ProCESS, ARISE, or ProMISe. Mandatory central venous saturation targets and protocolised transfusion are not used.
mustKnow.source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021

mustKnow.fact: If fluid and vasopressors do not restore stability, intravenous hydrocortisone at 200 mg per day is suggested. The ADRENAL trial did not reduce 90 day mortality. APROCCHSS, which added fludrocortisone, did reduce 90 day mortality. Fludrocortisone is not required by every guideline.
mustKnow.source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021

mustKnow.fact: HYPRESS found that hydrocortisone did not prevent progression from severe sepsis to shock. Steroids are not started just because the patient might become shocked.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 17

mustKnow.fact: LOVIT found that high dose intravenous vitamin C increased the risk of death or persistent organ dysfunction in septic adults. Vitamin C is not a sepsis drug.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 17

mustKnow.fact: Noradrenaline is started through a well watched peripheral line if central access would delay treatment of profound hypotension. The line is changed to central as soon as it is safe.
mustKnow.source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021

modules.name: Infections and antimicrobials in the ICU

topics.title: Infections and antimicrobials in the ICU
topics.book: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, infectious diseases section; Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 42

mustKnow.fact: Empiric cover for septic shock from a urinary or abdominal source includes a carbapenem or piperacillin tazobactam when extended spectrum beta lactamase organisms are likely. It is narrowed on the culture.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Sepsis and Septic Shock

mustKnow.fact: Carbapenem resistant Enterobacterales are treated with a drug the isolate is susceptible to, such as ceftazidime avibactam when the mechanism matches. Dual carbapenem therapy is not a default.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Nosocomial Pneumonia

mustKnow.fact: Acinetobacter baumannii treatment follows the susceptibility report. Colistin is a last resort because of nephrotoxicity and poor lung levels. Source control of an infected line or collection matters more than adding a third drug.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Nosocomial Pneumonia

mustKnow.fact: Invasive candidiasis is suspected in a septic patient with risk factors who does not improve on antibacterial drugs. An echinocandin is the empiric start. Fluconazole is for a susceptible isolate in a stable patient.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Invasive Fungal Infection

mustKnow.fact: A central line associated bloodstream infection is prevented by a checklist: sterile insertion, chlorhexidine skin preparation, and daily review of whether the line is still needed. The line is removed if it is the source.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Bacteremia and Catheter-Related Bloodstream Infections

mustKnow.fact: Catheter associated urinary infection is avoided by removing the urinary catheter. A positive culture without symptoms is colonisation and is not treated, except in pregnancy or before a urological procedure.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 42

mustKnow.fact: Procalcitonin can support stopping antibiotics when the clinical course is good. It does not start antibiotics, and it does not overrule a concerning examination.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Infection Prevention in the Intensive Care Unit

mustKnow.fact: Augmented renal clearance, a creatinine clearance above about 130 mL/min in young trauma or neurosurgical patients, underdoses renally cleared antibiotics. The dose is increased or the level is measured. A normal creatinine does not mean a normal clearance.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Bacteremia and Catheter-Related Bloodstream Infections

topics.title: Tropical infections in the ICU
topics.book: WHO Guidelines for malaria; national programme practice. No tropical chapter in Marino 5e or Washington Manual 4e.

mustKnow.fact: Severe falciparum malaria is treated with intravenous artesunate, 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, and 24 hours, then daily until the patient can take oral treatment. Quinine is the alternative only when artesunate is unavailable.
mustKnow.source: WHO Guidelines for malaria

mustKnow.fact: Severe malaria includes cerebral malaria, shock, acidosis, severe anaemia, hypoglycaemia, renal failure, and pulmonary oedema. Hypoglycaemia is checked often because quinine and the disease both cause it.
mustKnow.source: WHO Guidelines for malaria

mustKnow.fact: Severe dengue leaks plasma. Fluid is titrated to perfusion and haematocrit, and it is stopped when the leak reverses, or the patient is pushed into pulmonary oedema. There is no routine bolus for every high haematocrit.
mustKnow.source: National dengue management guidance

mustKnow.fact: Scrub typhus is treated with doxycycline. An eschar is useful when present and is often absent. Delay in doxycycline is what makes the ICU course, not a missing eschar.
mustKnow.source: National programme practice for scrub typhus

mustKnow.fact: Leptospirosis with Weil disease or pulmonary haemorrhage is treated with penicillin or ceftriaxone, plus support of the lung and the kidney. Conjunctival suffusion and calf tenderness are clinical clues.
mustKnow.source: National programme practice for leptospirosis

mustKnow.fact: Melioidosis, Burkholderia pseudomallei, needs prolonged eradication after the intensive phase. It is in the differential of community sepsis in endemic districts, and ordinary short course antibiotics relapse.
mustKnow.source: National programme practice for melioidosis

mustKnow.fact: Tetanus autonomic storms are treated in a quiet room, with magnesium, benzodiazepines, and wound care. Metronidazole is preferred to penicillin. Human tetanus immunoglobulin neutralises unbound toxin.
mustKnow.source: National programme practice for tetanus

mustKnow.fact: Rabies encephalitic disease is fatal once it is clinically established. ICU care is palliative unless the case meets a published treatment protocol in a specialist centre. Post exposure prophylaxis is the intervention that works, and it is given before symptoms.
mustKnow.source: WHO rabies clinical guidance

modules.name: Acute kidney injury in critical illness

topics.title: Acute kidney injury in critical illness
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 34 Acute Kidney Injury; KDIGO AKI guideline 2012; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Kidney Injury

mustKnow.fact: KDIGO stage 1 is creatinine 1.5 to 1.9 times baseline or a rise of at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 to 12 hours.
mustKnow.source: KDIGO AKI guideline 2012

mustKnow.fact: KDIGO stage 2 is creatinine 2.0 to 2.9 times baseline, or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 12 hours or more. Stage 3 is 3 times baseline, creatinine at least 4 mg/dL, renal replacement, urine output below 0.3 mL/kg/h for 24 hours, or anuria for 12 hours.
mustKnow.source: KDIGO AKI guideline 2012

mustKnow.fact: The PRESERVE trial found no benefit of sodium bicarbonate or N-acetylcysteine for contrast exposure. Volume expansion is the prevention used for an eGFR below 30. Metformin is held around the exposure.
mustKnow.source: KDIGO AKI guideline 2012

mustKnow.fact: Rhabdomyolysis is treated with early isotonic fluid. A creatine kinase in the tens of thousands supports the diagnosis. Alkalinisation of the urine is optional and is stopped if it causes hypocalcaemia. Compartment syndrome is a surgical diagnosis.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 34

mustKnow.fact: Cardiorenal syndrome type 1 is acute heart failure causing acute kidney injury. The treatment is the heart failure, not a fluid bolus given because the creatinine rose.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Decompensated Heart Failure

mustKnow.fact: Hepatorenal syndrome AKI is a diagnosis of exclusion in cirrhosis. Terlipressin plus albumin improves reversal. The CONFIRM trial also showed more respiratory failure, so the patient is watched for pulmonary oedema.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, End-Stage Liver Disease

mustKnow.fact: A furosemide stress test gives 1 mg/kg, or 1.5 mg/kg if the patient has had loop diuretics. Urine output below 200 mL in 2 hours predicts progression and a higher chance of needing renal replacement.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Kidney Injury

mustKnow.fact: NGAL and other biomarkers rise early. They do not replace KDIGO staging for the decision to start or withhold renal replacement.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Kidney Injury

modules.name: Renal replacement therapy in the ICU

topics.title: Renal replacement therapy in the ICU
topics.book: KDIGO AKI guideline 2012; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Renal Replacement Therapy

mustKnow.fact: STARRT-AKI found that accelerated renal replacement did not reduce mortality compared with a standard strategy, and more survivors remained dialysis dependent. AKIKI similarly supported waiting when there is no emergency indication.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Renal Replacement Therapy

mustKnow.fact: Emergency indications remain refractory hyperkalaemia, refractory acidosis, pulmonary oedema from fluid that diuretics cannot move, uraemic complications, and some dialysable toxins.
mustKnow.source: KDIGO AKI guideline 2012

mustKnow.fact: The delivered effluent dose for continuous therapy is 20 to 25 mL/kg/h. The RENAL trial, 25 versus 40, and the ATN trial, about 20 versus 35, found no benefit of a higher dose.
mustKnow.source: KDIGO AKI guideline 2012

mustKnow.fact: CVVH clears by convection, CVVHD by diffusion, and CVVHDF by both. Intermittent haemodialysis removes potassium faster in a stable patient. SLED is a hybrid used when continuous therapy is not available.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Renal Replacement Therapy

mustKnow.fact: KDIGO suggests regional citrate anticoagulation for continuous therapy when there is no contraindication. Citrate accumulation in liver failure or profound shock shows up as a rising total to ionised calcium ratio and a metabolic acidosis.
mustKnow.source: KDIGO AKI guideline 2012

mustKnow.fact: Filter clotting is caused by a high filtration fraction, slow blood flow, or a kinked catheter. Raising the replacement fluid without fixing access does not stop it.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Renal Replacement Therapy

mustKnow.fact: Drug dosing on continuous therapy must count residual kidney function and the effluent. Vancomycin and aminoglycosides are dosed with levels. A creatinine from yesterday is the wrong denominator.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Renal Replacement Therapy

mustKnow.fact: Continuous therapy causes less haemodynamic swing than intermittent dialysis and is chosen for an unstable patient. It does not improve mortality in trials that compared the two in patients who could tolerate either.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Renal Replacement Therapy

topics.title: Electrolyte disorders in the ICU
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 35 to Ch. 38; European hyponatraemia guideline 2014

mustKnow.fact: Severe symptoms of hyponatraemia, seizures or deep coma, are treated with a 100 to 150 mL bolus of 3% saline over 10 to 20 minutes, which can be repeated twice. The aim of the bolus is a rise of about 4 to 6 mmol/L.
mustKnow.source: European hyponatraemia guideline 2014
