mustKnow.fact: The European limit is a rise of at most 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and 8 mmol/L in the next 24 hours, with a tighter limit of 8 mmol/L in the first day for high risk patients. Overcorrection risks osmotic demyelination.
mustKnow.source: European hyponatraemia guideline 2014

mustKnow.fact: If sodium rises too fast, desmopressin and 5% dextrose are used to re-lower it. Free water restriction alone will not catch a rapid aquaresis.
mustKnow.source: European hyponatraemia guideline 2014

mustKnow.fact: Hypernatraemia is a free water deficit. The deficit is replaced slowly, usually no faster than 10 mmol/L per day, unless the rise was acute over minutes, as in salt poisoning.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 35

mustKnow.fact: ECG changes of hyperkalaemia are treated with intravenous calcium, which stabilises the membrane and does not lower the potassium. Insulin with glucose, and nebulised salbutamol, shift potassium inward. Removal is by diuretic, resin, or dialysis.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 36

mustKnow.fact: A standard shift dose is 10 units of regular insulin with 25 g of glucose. The glucose is checked for hours because hypoglycaemia outlasts the potassium fall.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 36

mustKnow.fact: Refeeding syndrome drops phosphate, potassium, and magnesium when carbohydrate is restarted. Thiamine is given first, calories are increased slowly, and phosphate is replaced before a cardiac arrhythmia.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 38

mustKnow.fact: Hypomagnesaemia causes refractory hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia. Magnesium is replaced before expecting the potassium to stay up. Deep tendon reflexes are watched when magnesium is infused.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 37

topics.title: Acid-base disorders
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 31 Acid-Base Analysis, Ch. 32 and Ch. 33

mustKnow.fact: The anion gap is sodium minus chloride minus bicarbonate. A normal gap is about 8 to 12. For every 1 g/dL that albumin is below 4, about 2.5 is added to the gap, or a low albumin hides a high gap acidosis.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 31

mustKnow.fact: Winter formula estimates the compensatory PaCO2 in metabolic acidosis as 1.5 times bicarbonate plus 8, plus or minus 2. A PaCO2 far from that means a second respiratory disorder.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 31

mustKnow.fact: The delta ratio compares the rise in anion gap with the fall in bicarbonate. A value near 1 fits a pure high gap acidosis. A low value means a coexisting normal gap acidosis.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 31

mustKnow.fact: The Stewart approach uses the strong ion difference. A large saline infusion narrows it by raising chloride and causes a hyperchloremic normal gap acidosis.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 31

mustKnow.fact: An osmolar gap above 10, with a high anion gap acidosis, suggests methanol or ethylene glycol until proved otherwise. Treatment is fomepizole and, when severe, dialysis. Do not wait for the level if the clinical picture fits.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 52

mustKnow.fact: Diabetic ketoacidosis and alcoholic or starvation ketoacidosis are high gap acidoses. Euglycaemic ketoacidosis on an SGLT2 inhibitor is missed if the clinician waits for a high glucose.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 32

mustKnow.fact: Chloride responsive metabolic alkalosis has a urine chloride below 20 mmol/L and is treated with chloride and volume. Chloride resistant alkalosis, urine chloride above 20, includes hyperaldosteronism and severe hypokalaemia.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 33

mustKnow.fact: A respiratory acidosis with a normal pH and a high bicarbonate is chronic. An acute rise in PaCO2 of 10 mmHg raises bicarbonate by only about 1 mmol/L. Using the chronic rule on an acute patient misses how severe the acidaemia will be.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Respiratory Acid-Base Disorders

topics.title: Endocrine emergencies in critical care
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 32 and Ch. 51; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Diabetic Ketoacidosis and Glucose Control

mustKnow.fact: Diabetic ketoacidosis is treated with fluid first. Insulin at 0.1 units/kg/h is started after potassium is known. If potassium is below 3.3 mmol/L, insulin is withheld until potassium is replaced. Bicarbonate is considered only if the pH is below 6.9.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Diabetic Ketoacidosis and Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State

mustKnow.fact: Dextrose is added when glucose falls to about 200 mg/dL, and insulin is continued until the anion gap closes. Stopping insulin when the glucose is normal leaves the ketoacidosis untreated.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Diabetic Ketoacidosis and Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State

mustKnow.fact: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state is more dehydrated and less acidotic than ketoacidosis. Fluid is the main treatment and insulin doses are smaller. Thrombosis risk is high.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Diabetic Ketoacidosis and Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State

mustKnow.fact: NICE-SUGAR showed that an intensive glucose target of 81 to 108 mg/dL increased mortality compared with a target of 180 mg/dL or less. Insulin is started when glucose is at or above 180 mg/dL, with a target of about 144 to 180.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Glucose Control in the Intensive Care Unit

mustKnow.fact: Critical illness related corticosteroid insufficiency is not diagnosed by a random cortisol. If septic shock needs high dose vasopressors after fluid, hydrocortisone is given without waiting for a stimulation test.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Adrenal Insufficiency in Critical Illness

mustKnow.fact: Adrenal crisis is shock with a suggestive history. Treatment is intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg and saline. Fludrocortisone is for confirmed primary adrenal failure after the crisis, not for the first hour.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Adrenal Insufficiency in Critical Illness

mustKnow.fact: Thyroid storm treatment is a beta blocker, a thionamide, then iodine at least an hour after the thionamide, plus a glucocorticoid. Propylthiouracil is preferred when available because it also blocks peripheral conversion. The trigger is treated.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Thyroid Disorders

mustKnow.fact: Myxoedema coma is treated with intravenous thyroid hormone and a stress dose glucocorticoid until adrenal failure is excluded. Rewarming is passive. Sedatives and hyponatraemia are common precipitants.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Thyroid Disorders

topics.title: Nutrition in critical illness
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 48 to Ch. 50; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Nutrition in the Intensive Care Unit

mustKnow.fact: Start enteral nutrition within 24 to 48 hours in a patient who is resuscitated and has a working gut. The gastric route is first. Post-pyloric feeding is for intolerance or high aspiration risk, not the default.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Nutrition in the Intensive Care Unit

mustKnow.fact: CALORIES found no mortality difference between the early parenteral route and the early enteral route. NUTRIREA-2 found more bowel ischaemia with early full dose enteral feeding in shocked patients, without a mortality benefit.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 49

mustKnow.fact: EDEN found that trophic enteral feeding for the first 6 days was not inferior to full enteral feeding for ventilator free days. Full calories on day 1 are not mandatory.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 49

mustKnow.fact: The EFFORT Protein trial found that a higher protein dose did not improve outcomes and may harm patients with acute kidney injury and high organ failure scores. More protein is not always better.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Nutrition in the Intensive Care Unit

mustKnow.fact: PERMIT found that permissive underfeeding of calories, with protein maintained, did not change mortality compared with full calorie feeding.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 48

mustKnow.fact: EPaNIC found that early supplemental parenteral nutrition increased infections compared with withholding it until day 8. Parenteral nutrition is not added on day 1 just to meet a calorie target.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 50

mustKnow.fact: A single gastric residual below 500 mL is not a reason to stop feeds. Prokinetics are tried before the tube is declared a failure. Residual checks are not required by routine.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Nutrition in the Intensive Care Unit

mustKnow.fact: Refeeding risk is highest in starved, alcoholic, and very underweight patients. Give thiamine, replace phosphate, potassium, and magnesium, and raise calories over several days.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 48

topics.title: Pharmacology in critical illness
topics.book: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Common Drug Dosages; Chang, Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation 4e Ch. 2

mustKnow.fact: Hydrophilic drugs such as aminoglycosides, vancomycin, and beta lactams have a larger volume of distribution in sepsis and after fluid. The loading dose is not reduced just because the creatinine is high.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Common Drug Dosages

mustKnow.fact: Augmented renal clearance above about 130 mL/min underdoses renally cleared antibiotics in young trauma and neurosurgical patients. A normal serum creatinine does not exclude it.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Common Drug Dosages

mustKnow.fact: Hypoalbuminaemia raises the free fraction of phenytoin and valproate. A total level looks low while the free level is adequate. Dose changes use the free level when it is available.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Common Drug Dosages

mustKnow.fact: High extraction drugs such as lidocaine are cleared by liver blood flow. Shock reduces their clearance. Low extraction drugs depend on enzyme activity and protein binding.
mustKnow.source: Chang, Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation 4e Ch. 2

mustKnow.fact: Cisatracurium is cleared by Hofmann elimination and does not depend on the kidney or the liver. It is the neuromuscular blocker chosen when those organs have failed. The metabolite laudanosine is less of a concern than with atracurium.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Common Drug Dosages

mustKnow.fact: Therapeutic drug monitoring is used for vancomycin, aminoglycosides, and, when available, beta lactam levels in prolonged shock. A standard ward dose is the wrong dose.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Common Drug Dosages

mustKnow.fact: Drug interactions in the ICU are dominated by azoles, amiodarone, macrolides, and enzyme inducers such as rifampicin and phenytoin. The QT interval and calcineurin inhibitor levels are checked when those drugs are combined.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Drug-Drug Interactions

mustKnow.fact: Renal dose adjustment applies to maintenance doses, not automatically to the first dose of a hydrophilic antibiotic in sepsis. Underdosing the first day is a common error.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Common Drug Dosages

sections.name: Gastrointestinal, hepatic and haematological critical care

modules.name: Acute liver failure and acute on chronic liver failure

topics.title: Acute liver failure and acute on chronic liver failure
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 39 Liver Failure; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Liver Failure and End-Stage Liver Disease

mustKnow.fact: King's College paracetamol criteria for transplant listing are an arterial pH below 7.3 after resuscitation, or all three of INR above 6.5, creatinine above 3.4 mg/dL, and grade 3 or 4 encephalopathy.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Liver Failure

mustKnow.fact: Non-paracetamol King's College criteria are an INR above 6.5, or any three of age under 10 or over 40, a drug or indeterminate cause, jaundice to encephalopathy longer than 7 days, INR above 3.5, and bilirubin above 17 mg/dL.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Liver Failure

mustKnow.fact: N-acetylcysteine is given for paracetamol acute liver failure even when presentation is late. It is also reasonable in non-paracetamol acute liver failure. It does not replace transplant assessment.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Liver Failure

mustKnow.fact: An arterial ammonia above about 200 micromol/L is associated with cerebral oedema in acute liver failure. Management is head-up positioning, normothermia, osmotherapy, and avoidance of hyponatraemia. Lactulose alone does not treat this oedema.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Liver Failure

mustKnow.fact: Acute on chronic liver failure is graded by the number of organ failures on the CLIF organ failure score. Prognosis is worse than a simple decompensation with the same bilirubin.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, End-Stage Liver Disease

mustKnow.fact: Variceal bleeding is treated with a vasoactive drug, terlipressin or octreotide, plus an antibiotic, plus early endoscopy. A restrictive transfusion target near 7 g/dL is used unless the patient is exsanguinating.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Gastrointestinal Bleeding

mustKnow.fact: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is treated with a third generation cephalosporin. Albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3 is given when creatinine is above 1 mg/dL, urea is above 30 mg/dL, or bilirubin is above 4 mg/dL.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, End-Stage Liver Disease

mustKnow.fact: High volume plasma exchange can improve transplant free survival in acute liver failure. It is a bridge, not a cure, and it is done in a transplant centre.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Liver Failure

modules.name: GI bleeding and stress ulcer prophylaxis

topics.title: GI bleeding and stress ulcer prophylaxis
topics.book: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Gastrointestinal Bleeding; Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 4 Alimentary Prophylaxis

mustKnow.fact: A Glasgow-Blatchford score of 0 or 1 identifies very low risk upper gastrointestinal bleeding that can often avoid admission. Rockall scoring needs the endoscopy and is not the admission score.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Gastrointestinal Bleeding

mustKnow.fact: Villanueva showed that a restrictive transfusion threshold of 7 g/dL improved outcomes compared with a liberal threshold in upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Massive bleeding and ischaemic heart disease are the debated exceptions.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Gastrointestinal Bleeding

mustKnow.fact: After endoscopic haemostasis of a high risk ulcer, an intravenous proton pump inhibitor is given. The examined continuous regimen is 80 mg then 8 mg per hour for 72 hours. Intermittent high dose therapy is an acceptable alternative.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Gastrointestinal Bleeding

mustKnow.fact: HALT-IT found that tranexamic acid did not reduce death from gastrointestinal bleeding and increased venous thrombosis. It is not given for this indication.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Gastrointestinal Bleeding

mustKnow.fact: Early TIPS is considered for Child-Pugh C cirrhosis below 14 points, or Child-Pugh B with active bleeding, after initial control of variceal haemorrhage.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Gastrointestinal Bleeding

mustKnow.fact: A Sengstaken-Blakemore tube is a bridge to endoscopy or TIPS in exsanguinating variceal bleeding. The airway is protected first. The balloon is not left inflated as definitive treatment.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Gastrointestinal Bleeding

mustKnow.fact: SUP-ICU found that pantoprazole did not reduce 90 day mortality in ICU patients at risk of stress ulceration, and it did reduce clinically important bleeding. Prophylaxis is for high risk patients, not for every ICU admission.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 4

mustKnow.fact: Lower gastrointestinal bleeding is usually self limited. Unstable patients are resuscitated like upper bleeding and go to CT angiography when endoscopy of the stomach has not found the source.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Gastrointestinal Bleeding

topics.title: Severe acute pancreatitis
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 40 Acute Pancreatitis; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Pancreatitis

mustKnow.fact: Revised Atlanta classifies acute pancreatitis as mild, moderately severe when organ failure lasts under 48 hours or a local complication is present, and severe when organ failure persists beyond 48 hours.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Pancreatitis

mustKnow.fact: WATERFALL stopped early because aggressive fluid, a large bolus then 3 mL/kg/h, caused more fluid overload than a moderate strategy without improving outcomes. Moderate fluid is the practice.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 40

mustKnow.fact: Early enteral feeding is safe and is preferred to parenteral nutrition. Prophylactic antibiotics do not prevent infection of necrosis and are not given for every pancreatitis.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 40

mustKnow.fact: The PANTER trial supported a step-up approach: delay, then percutaneous or endoscopic drainage, then necrosectomy only if needed. Open necrosectomy is not the first operation.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Pancreatitis

mustKnow.fact: Intervention for infected necrosis is delayed to about 4 weeks when the patient can be stabilised, so that the collection becomes walled off. Deterioration overrides the calendar.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Pancreatitis

mustKnow.fact: Abdominal compartment syndrome is sought when ventilation or urine output worsens. A bladder pressure above 20 mmHg with new organ failure defines it.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 40

mustKnow.fact: Gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction needs urgent ERCP. ERCP is not routine for every gallstone pancreatitis without those features.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Pancreatitis

mustKnow.fact: Severity prediction with Ranson or APACHE does not change the first day of care. Organ failure on the ward round does. Lactate, urine output, and oxygen need are the practical monitors.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 40

modules.name: Coagulopathy and haematology in the ICU

topics.title: Coagulopathy and haematology in the ICU
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 13 Platelets and Plasma; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Thrombocytopenia and Coagulopathy

mustKnow.fact: The ISTH overt DIC score uses platelets, fibrin markers, prothrombin time, and fibrinogen. A score of 5 or more is compatible with overt DIC. Treat the cause. Plasma is for bleeding or a procedure, not for a number.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Management of the Bleeding Patient/Coagulopathy

mustKnow.fact: Heparin induced thrombocytopenia is suspected with the 4T score. A score of 3 or less makes it unlikely. A score of 6 or more is high probability. Heparin is stopped, and argatroban or another non-heparin anticoagulant is started. Warfarin is not started alone while platelets are low.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Thrombocytopenia in the Intensive Care Unit

mustKnow.fact: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is microangiopathic haemolysis with thrombocytopenia and an ADAMTS13 activity below 10%. Plasma exchange is urgent. Caplacizumab is added where available. Platelets are not transfused unless there is life threatening bleeding.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Thrombocytopenia in the Intensive Care Unit

mustKnow.fact: The PROTECT trial found that dalteparin reduced pulmonary embolism compared with unfractionated heparin in critically ill patients, with similar bleeding and mortality. Pharmacological prophylaxis is the default unless bleeding forbids it.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Hypercoagulable States

mustKnow.fact: Warfarin reversal for major bleeding is four factor prothrombin complex concentrate plus vitamin K, not plasma first. Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran. Andexanet is the specific option for factor Xa inhibitors when it is available, and it has a thrombotic risk.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Management of the Bleeding Patient/Coagulopathy

mustKnow.fact: Protamine reverses unfractionated heparin fully and low molecular weight heparin only partly. The dose is limited to what is needed because excess protamine is itself an anticoagulant.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Management of the Bleeding Patient/Coagulopathy

mustKnow.fact: A platelet count below 10 x 10 to the 9 per litre is a common prophylactic transfusion threshold in a stable patient. A threshold near 50 is used before major surgery, and near 100 before neurosurgery. Immune thrombocytopenia is not transfused to a number.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Thrombocytopenia in the Intensive Care Unit

mustKnow.fact: Sepsis induced coagulopathy and overt DIC are not indications for therapeutic heparin unless a clot is present. Prophylactic heparin is continued if platelets and bleeding allow.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Management of the Bleeding Patient/Coagulopathy

topics.title: Transfusion medicine and blood products
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 12 and Ch. 13; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Transfusion Practices

mustKnow.fact: The default ICU haemoglobin threshold is 7 g/dL, from TRICC and from TRISS in septic shock. Transfusion above that needs a reason, such as acute bleeding or an unstable coronary syndrome.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 12

mustKnow.fact: MINT did not show that a restrictive strategy was superior to a liberal strategy in acute myocardial infarction. Coronary disease is the situation where the threshold is individualised rather than copied from TRICC.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 12

mustKnow.fact: TRALI is non-cardiogenic oedema during or within 6 hours of transfusion, from donor antibody or bioactive lipids. Treatment is oxygen and stopping the product. Diuretic is not the treatment.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Transfusion Practices

mustKnow.fact: TACO is hydrostatic oedema from the volume and rate of transfusion, often with hypertension. It is treated as heart failure, and the next unit is given more slowly.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Transfusion Practices

mustKnow.fact: Fresh frozen plasma does not reliably correct a mildly raised INR and is not given to a non-bleeding patient for an INR of 1.5 before a routine procedure.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 13

mustKnow.fact: Cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate is the replacement for a low fibrinogen. Plasma is a poor fibrinogen source because of the volume required.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 13

mustKnow.fact: A competent Jehovah's Witness refusal of blood is respected. Iron, erythropoietin, and cell salvage are discussed. Blood is not given in secret.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Transfusion Practices

mustKnow.fact: One unit of red cells in an adult raises haemoglobin by about 1 g/dL. Ordering two units by habit is an outdated reflex. Reassess after one unit when the patient is not exsanguinating.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 12

topics.title: Traumatic brain injury
topics.book: Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines, 4th edition, 2016; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Traumatic Brain Injury and Elevated Intracranial Pressure

mustKnow.fact: A single episode of hypoxia or hypotension doubles the harm of a traumatic brain injury. Airway, oxygen, and blood pressure come before the CT scanner.
mustKnow.source: Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines, 4th edition, 2016

mustKnow.fact: Treat intracranial pressure above 22 mmHg. Keep cerebral perfusion pressure between 60 and 70 mmHg. Do not push cerebral perfusion pressure higher by routine vasopressors.
mustKnow.source: Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines, 4th edition, 2016

mustKnow.fact: Hyperosmolar therapy is mannitol 0.25 to 1 g/kg or a bolus of 3% saline, commonly about 150 mL. Mannitol is held when serum osmolality is above 320 mOsm/kg. Choose saline when the patient is hypotensive.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Traumatic Brain Injury and Elevated Intracranial Pressure

mustKnow.fact: The CRASH trial showed that corticosteroids increased mortality in traumatic brain injury. Steroids are not used for the brain injury.
mustKnow.source: Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines, 4th edition, 2016

mustKnow.fact: DECRA found that early decompressive craniectomy for diffuse injury lowered intracranial pressure and worsened functional outcome. RESCUEicp, using craniectomy as a last tier, lowered mortality and increased survival with severe disability.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Traumatic Brain Injury and Elevated Intracranial Pressure

mustKnow.fact: EUROTHERM found that hypothermia used as a stage of intracranial pressure treatment worsened outcome. Routine hypothermia is not used.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Traumatic Brain Injury and Elevated Intracranial Pressure

mustKnow.fact: Phenytoin or levetiracetam for 7 days prevents early post traumatic seizures. Prolonged prophylaxis does not prevent late epilepsy and is not continued by habit.
mustKnow.source: Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines, 4th edition, 2016

mustKnow.fact: The Glasgow coma scale is repeated and the motor score is recorded. A dilated pupil with a falling score is a surgical emergency until a CT shows otherwise.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Traumatic Brain Injury and Elevated Intracranial Pressure

topics.title: Stroke, subarachnoid and intracerebral haemorrhage
topics.book: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Ischemic Stroke, Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage, and Intracerebral Hemorrhage

mustKnow.fact: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage is secured early by coiling or clipping. Nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours by mouth for 21 days reduces poor outcome. Intravenous nimodipine is not the regimen because of hypotension.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage

mustKnow.fact: Delayed cerebral ischaemia is a clinical diagnosis, not an angiogram alone. Induced hypertension is used after the aneurysm is secured. Haemodilution and hypervolaemia, the old triple H, are not.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage

mustKnow.fact: Before the aneurysm is secured, systolic pressure is usually kept below 160 mmHg. After securing, a higher pressure is allowed to treat delayed ischaemia.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage

mustKnow.fact: Hunt and Hess and WFNS grades describe clinical severity. The modified Fisher scale uses the thickness of blood and intraventricular blood to estimate vasospasm risk.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage

mustKnow.fact: INTERACT2 lowered systolic pressure toward 140 mmHg in intracerebral haemorrhage. The primary dichotomous outcome was not significant, and the ordinal shift was favourable. ATACH-2, aiming even lower, showed no benefit and more renal adverse events.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Intracerebral Hemorrhage

mustKnow.fact: Anticoagulation is reversed immediately in intracerebral haemorrhage. Warfarin receives prothrombin complex concentrate and vitamin K. Do not wait for the INR to come back before ordering the reversal if the history is clear.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Intracerebral Hemorrhage

mustKnow.fact: Thrombolysis for ischaemic stroke follows the time window and imaging criteria of the current stroke guideline, and blood pressure is lowered below 185/110 mmHg before the drug. Thrombectomy is for large vessel occlusion inside the eligible window, including selected late presenters with favourable imaging.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Ischemic Stroke

mustKnow.fact: A cerebellar haemorrhage or infarct with hydrocephalus or a falling conscious level needs surgical decompression. It is not watched on a ward.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Intracerebral Hemorrhage

topics.title: Status epilepticus
topics.book: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Status Epilepticus

mustKnow.fact: First line treatment is a benzodiazepine: intravenous lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg, or intramuscular midazolam when there is no line. Underdosing the benzodiazepine is the common error.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Status Epilepticus

mustKnow.fact: RAMPART showed that intramuscular midazolam was at least as effective as intravenous lorazepam in the prehospital setting. Do not delay the first dose to place a drip.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Status Epilepticus

mustKnow.fact: ESETT found that levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, and valproate were equivalent as the second line drug. One of them is given immediately after the benzodiazepine, at a full loading dose.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Status Epilepticus

mustKnow.fact: Refractory status epilepticus, continuing after benzodiazepine and a second drug, is treated with a midazolam or propofol infusion and continuous EEG. Ketamine is an adjunct when those fail.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Status Epilepticus

mustKnow.fact: Super refractory status continues despite 24 hours of anaesthetic infusion. The search turns to autoimmune encephalitis, a missed metabolic cause, and a specialist anaesthetic plan.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Status Epilepticus

mustKnow.fact: Nonconvulsive status is in the differential of unexplained coma after a convulsion. EEG makes the diagnosis. A normal CT does not exclude it.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Status Epilepticus

mustKnow.fact: Glucose is checked at once. Hyponatraemia, hypoxia, and a toxic alcohol are treated as causes, not as spectators, while the seizure drugs are given.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Status Epilepticus

mustKnow.fact: Valproate is avoided in known mitochondrial disease, pregnancy when an alternative exists, and significant liver failure. Fosphenytoin causes hypotension and is given with monitoring.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Status Epilepticus

topics.title: Brain death and organ donation
topics.book: Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act and Rules; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Declaration of Brain Death

mustKnow.fact: Brainstem death requires a known irreversible cause, a deep coma, exclusion of confounders, absent brainstem reflexes, and an apnoea test. Confounders include temperature below 36 C is not the rule: the patient is warmed to at least 36 C, sedatives have cleared, and sodium and glucose are not extreme.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Declaration of Brain Death

mustKnow.fact: The apnoea test starts from a PaCO2 near 40 mmHg. The patient is preoxygenated and disconnected. The test supports brain death when there is no breath and PaCO2 is at least 60 mmHg or has risen by at least 20 mmHg.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Declaration of Brain Death

mustKnow.fact: Indian rules require two examinations by a board of doctors who are not the transplant retrieval team, separated by at least 6 hours in adults. The form is the legal record.
mustKnow.source: Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Rules

mustKnow.fact: Ancillary tests, four vessel angiography, radionuclide scan, or EEG, are used only when a clinical part cannot be completed, such as a failed apnoea test from hypoxia. They are not a shortcut past an unfinished examination.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Declaration of Brain Death

mustKnow.fact: Spinal reflexes, including Lazarus sign, can persist and do not exclude brain death. They are explained to the family before they are misread as life.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Declaration of Brain Death

mustKnow.fact: A vegetative state and brain death are not the same. A vegetative state has a sleep wake cycle and brainstem function. Brain death has neither.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Coma

mustKnow.fact: Donor management after consent uses lung protective ventilation, treatment of diabetes insipidus with vasopressin, and replacement of cortisol. The goal is organ perfusion, not a new diagnosis.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Management of the Organ Donor

mustKnow.fact: The family conversation about donation is separated from the declaration of death. The certifying doctors are not the retrieving surgeons.
mustKnow.source: Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act

modules.name: Neuromuscular emergencies and ICU acquired weakness

topics.title: Neuromuscular emergencies and ICU acquired weakness
topics.book: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Neuromuscular Disorders in the Critically Ill; Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 46

mustKnow.fact: Guillain-Barre syndrome is treated with intravenous immunoglobulin 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days, or with plasma exchange. Steroids do not help. Combining immunoglobulin and exchange is not better than either alone.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Neuromuscular Disorders in the Critically Ill

mustKnow.fact: Intubation in Guillain-Barre is considered at the 20, 30, 40 thresholds: vital capacity below 20 mL/kg, inspiratory pressure worse than minus 30 cmH2O, or expiratory pressure below 40 cmH2O, or when bulbar weakness threatens the airway.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Neuromuscular Disorders in the Critically Ill

mustKnow.fact: Myasthenic crisis is treated with plasma exchange or immunoglobulin, and the cholinesterase inhibitor is held if cholinergic signs are present. Drugs that worsen myasthenia, including aminoglycosides and magnesium, are avoided.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Neuromuscular Disorders in the Critically Ill

mustKnow.fact: Critical illness polyneuropathy is an axonal sensorimotor neuropathy. Critical illness myopathy shows myosin loss and is linked to steroids and neuromuscular blockers. Both cause failure to wean.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 46

mustKnow.fact: ICU acquired weakness is an MRC sum score below 48 out of 60 when the patient can be tested. Prevention is light sedation, less steroid and paralysis, and glucose control, not a specific drug.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 46

mustKnow.fact: Organophosphate poisoning causes an acute cholinergic crisis, an intermediate syndrome at 1 to 4 days with proximal and respiratory weakness, and a later neuropathy. The intermediate syndrome is why the patient is not extubated the moment the pupils look better.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 53

mustKnow.fact: Botulism descends, with pupils often involved, and sensation spared. Guillain-Barre ascends, with areflexia. The difference decides antitoxin versus immunoglobulin.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Neuromuscular Disorders in the Critically Ill

mustKnow.fact: Neuromuscular blockers are stopped daily and are not a sedation substitute. Prolonged blockade plus steroids is the setting for critical illness myopathy.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 46

topics.title: Analgesia, sedation and delirium
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 6 Analgesia and Sedation; PADIS guidelines 2018; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Sedation and Delirium

mustKnow.fact: Analgesia comes before sedation. Pain is treated with an opioid, and the sedation target is light, a RASS of 0 to minus 2, unless prone ventilation or intracranial pressure control requires deeper sedation.
mustKnow.source: PADIS guidelines, 2018

mustKnow.fact: SPICE III found no overall 90 day mortality benefit of dexmedetomidine as the primary sedative. Bradycardia and hypotension were more common. It remains useful when the goal is a lighter, more interactive patient.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Sedation and Delirium

mustKnow.fact: MENDS2 found no difference in delirium or other major outcomes between dexmedetomidine and propofol. Either is acceptable. Benzodiazepines are associated with more delirium and are not the routine infusion.
mustKnow.source: PADIS guidelines, 2018

mustKnow.fact: Propofol infusion syndrome is metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hypertriglyceridaemia, bradycardia, and renal failure, usually at doses above 4 mg/kg/h for more than 48 hours. The infusion is stopped.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 6

mustKnow.fact: CAM-ICU is the screening tool. Delirium is hypoactive more often than agitated, so a quiet patient is not assumed to be comfortable.
mustKnow.source: PADIS guidelines, 2018

mustKnow.fact: MIND-USA found that haloperidol or ziprasidone did not shorten delirium compared with placebo. Haloperidol is for dangerous agitation, not a treatment of delirium itself. AID-ICU did not show a gain in days alive and out of hospital.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Sedation and Delirium

mustKnow.fact: Rivastigmine increased mortality in one ICU delirium trial and is not used. Melatonin is not a proven preventive.
mustKnow.source: PADIS guidelines, 2018

mustKnow.fact: Daily awakening, or a protocol that keeps sedation light, is paired with a breathing trial. A continuous benzodiazepine infusion with no holiday is an outdated default.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 6

topics.title: Trauma critical care
topics.book: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Trauma Care for the Intensive Care Unit and Acute Spinal Cord Disorders

mustKnow.fact: The trauma primary survey treats catastrophic external bleeding and the airway together, then breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure. The cervical spine stays immobilised until it is cleared. A full history is not required before those first actions.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Trauma Care for the Intensive Care Unit

mustKnow.fact: A tertiary survey is a repeated head to toe examination within 24 hours, after resuscitation, looking for injuries missed in the first hour. It is written down. A normal first pass does not retire the search.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Trauma Care for the Intensive Care Unit

mustKnow.fact: Acute traumatic coagulopathy is present on arrival and is driven by shock and tissue injury, not only by later dilution. Damage control surgery packs bleeding and closes temporarily when the lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy is underway. Crystalloid is limited. Physiology is corrected in the ICU before definitive reconstruction.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Trauma Care for the Intensive Care Unit

mustKnow.fact: An open-book pelvic fracture in a shocked patient gets a pelvic binder centred over the greater trochanters, not over the iliac crests. The patient then goes to haemorrhage control. A long CT tour is not the next step while the blood pressure is still falling.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Trauma Care for the Intensive Care Unit

mustKnow.fact: The hypoxia of a flail chest is the pulmonary contusion underneath, not the paradoxical movement alone. Analgesia, including an epidural in a selected patient, and non-invasive ventilation are tried if the airway is safe. Intubate when the patient tires. Surgical fixation is for a chest wall that is still failing despite that care, not for every broken rib.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Trauma Care for the Intensive Care Unit

mustKnow.fact: Intra-abdominal hypertension is a sustained bladder pressure of 12 mmHg or more. Abdominal compartment syndrome is a pressure above 20 mmHg with new organ failure. Measure at end expiration in the supine patient. Sedation, nasogastric drainage, and treating ascites come before laparotomy, unless the abdomen is already the reason the patient is dying.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Trauma Care for the Intensive Care Unit

mustKnow.fact: Fat embolism usually appears 24 to 72 hours after a long-bone or pelvic fracture, with hypoxia, confusion, and petechiae on the conjunctiva or the axilla. Treatment is oxygen and fixation of the fracture. There is no specific drug, and steroids are not a routine antidote.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Trauma Care for the Intensive Care Unit

mustKnow.fact: Neurogenic shock is hypotension with bradycardia from a high spinal cord injury, usually above T6, and it is treated with a vasopressor and sometimes atropine. Spinal shock is a temporary loss of reflexes below the lesion. They are not the same, and neither is haemorrhagic shock. High-dose methylprednisolone is not routine. A crushed limb releases potassium and myoglobin when it is freed, so isotonic fluid is running before release and a tight compartment gets a fasciotomy.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Acute Spinal Cord Disorders

topics.title: Burns and inhalation injury
topics.book: ATLS and American Burn Association fluid practice. Marino 5e and Washington Manual 4e have no burns chapter.

mustKnow.fact: Parkland resuscitation starts at 4 mL of lactated Ringer's solution per kilogram per percent of body surface burned. Half is given in the first 8 hours from the time of the burn, and the rest over the next 16 hours. Adult urine output is titrated to about 0.5 mL/kg/h, and about 1 mL/kg/h in a small child. If the urine output is already adequate, the rest of the calculated volume is not forced in.
mustKnow.source: American Burn Association resuscitation practice

mustKnow.fact: Chasing the Parkland number after the urine output is adequate is fluid creep. The extra oedema can close the airway and can cause abdominal compartment syndrome. The formula is a starting estimate, timed from the injury, not a quota to be finished.
mustKnow.source: American Burn Association resuscitation practice

mustKnow.fact: The rule of nines assigns 9 percent to the head, 9 percent to each arm, 18 percent to each leg, 18 percent to the front of the trunk, and 18 percent to the back, with 1 percent for the perineum. The patient's palm is about 1 percent and is used for scattered burns.
mustKnow.source: ATLS burn size estimation

mustKnow.fact: A threatened airway from inhalation injury is intubated early, before oedema closes it. Soot, hoarseness, stridor, or deep burns of the face are the triggers. Bronchoscopy grades the injury after the tube is in. It is not the first test in a patient who is already stridulous.
mustKnow.source: ATLS inhalation injury practice

mustKnow.fact: Pulse oximetry cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin. A co-oximeter measures it. One hundred percent oxygen is started at once. The half-life of carboxyhaemoglobin is about 4 hours on room air and about 1 hour on 100 percent oxygen. Hyperbaric oxygen is considered for coma, cardiac ischaemia, pregnancy, or a very high level, and it is not a reason to delay oxygen or the airway.
mustKnow.source: ATLS inhalation injury practice

mustKnow.fact: Smoke inhalation with a lactic acidosis worse than the oxygen problem suggests cyanide from burning synthetics. Hydroxocobalamin 5 g intravenously is the antidote. Nitrites are a poor choice when carbon monoxide is also present, because they form methaemoglobin and reduce oxygen carriage further.
mustKnow.source: ATLS inhalation injury practice

mustKnow.fact: A circumferential full-thickness burn of a limb or of the chest can act as a tourniquet. Escharotomy incises the eschar to restore perfusion or chest movement. It is a bedside procedure when those signs are present. It is not a fasciotomy, which is for a muscle compartment.
mustKnow.source: ATLS burn practice

mustKnow.fact: Burn wound colonisation is expected. Wound sepsis is a change in the wound plus fever and new organ dysfunction. Early excision and grafting is the source control. The hypermetabolism after a major burn lasts weeks, so enteral feeding starts early. The Parkland calculation is not a diet.
mustKnow.source: American Burn Association resuscitation practice

topics.title: Poisoning in the ICU
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 52 and Ch. 53; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Toxicology

mustKnow.fact: Organophosphate poisoning is treated with atropine until the chest is dry, doubling the dose every few minutes. Pralidoxime is added early, before the enzyme has aged, and it is most useful for nicotinic weakness. A clear chest is the endpoint. Carbamate poisoning needs atropine. Pralidoxime is not required for a pure carbamate.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Toxicology

mustKnow.fact: Paraquat has no antidote. Charcoal is reasonable early if the airway is protected. The lung injury is progressive fibrosis. Supplemental oxygen can worsen that injury, so the lowest inspired oxygen that keeps an acceptable saturation is used. A small swallow of the concentrated liquid is often fatal, and the mouth burns are the clue.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 53

mustKnow.fact: Aluminium phosphide releases phosphine and causes refractory shock and metabolic acidosis. There is no specific antidote. Magnesium is often infused in Indian practice and has not been shown to reduce death. The airway and the circulation are treated directly. A lavage ritual is not a reason to delay that support.
mustKnow.source: Standard Indian toxicology practice for a poison not covered as a chapter in Marino 5e or Washington Manual 4e

mustKnow.fact: N-acetylcysteine is started when the 4 hour paracetamol level is above the treatment line, or immediately if the presentation is late or the overdose was staggered. The intravenous course is 150 mg/kg over 1 hour, then 50 mg/kg over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours. The clock starts from the time of ingestion, and a late start is still worthwhile in liver injury.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 52

mustKnow.fact: Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase in methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning. The load is 15 mg/kg, then 10 mg/kg every 12 hours while dialysis is not running. The interval is shortened during haemodialysis because the drug is removed. Dialysis is added for visual symptoms, refractory acidosis, renal failure, or a very high level. Ethanol is only the fallback when fomepizole is unavailable.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 53

mustKnow.fact: Tricyclic antidepressant toxicity widens the QRS by sodium channel blockade. Sodium bicarbonate is given when the QRS is wider than 100 ms, or when there is a ventricular arrhythmia or hypotension. The pH is taken to about 7.45 to 7.55. Seizures are stopped with a benzodiazepine. Phenytoin is avoided, because it blocks the same channel.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 52

mustKnow.fact: Calcium channel blocker shock is treated with calcium and with high-dose insulin, about 1 unit/kg as a bolus and then 1 unit/kg/h, plus dextrose so the glucose stays safe. Lipid emulsion 20 percent, 1.5 mL/kg as a bolus, is the rescue for local anaesthetic systemic toxicity and a late adjunct in this poisoning. Vasopressors support the pressure while those treatments act.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Toxicology

mustKnow.fact: Digoxin specific antibody fragments are given for a life-threatening arrhythmia, a potassium above 5 mmol/L, or renal failure with clear digoxin toxicity. Calcium is not the treatment of that hyperkalaemia. EXTRIP dialysis is for a small, poorly protein bound toxin, including severe salicylate, lithium, metformin lactic acidosis, theophylline, and valproate. Intermittent haemodialysis clears them faster than continuous therapy when the blood pressure allows. Salicylate is also alkalinised with bicarbonate while dialysis is arranged.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 52

topics.title: Envenomation
topics.book: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare national snakebite protocol; standard Indian scorpion and anaphylaxis practice. No snakebite chapter in Marino 5e or Washington Manual 4e.

mustKnow.fact: Systemic envenoming, not a pair of fang marks alone, is the indication for anti-snake venom. The 20 minute whole blood clotting test is incoagulable in a viper bite with coagulopathy. Progressive neurotoxicity is the other indication. Local swelling that is not progressing does not by itself demand venom.
mustKnow.source: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare national snakebite protocol

mustKnow.fact: Indian polyvalent anti-snake venom covers the cobra, the common krait, Russell's viper, and the saw-scaled viper. It does not cover the hump-nosed pit viper. More vials cannot neutralise a venom the product does not contain.
mustKnow.source: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare national snakebite protocol

mustKnow.fact: The usual initial dose for systemic envenoming is 10 vials, infused, with no subcutaneous test dose. A test dose does not predict anaphylaxis and it delays treatment. If the 20 minute whole blood clotting test is still abnormal at 6 hours, or if neurotoxic signs progress, a further dose is considered.
mustKnow.source: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare national snakebite protocol

mustKnow.fact: Anaphylaxis to anti-snake venom is treated by stopping the infusion and giving intramuscular adrenaline. The venom is restarted, once the reaction has settled, if systemic envenoming continues. There is no test dose that makes anaphylaxis impossible.
mustKnow.source: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare national snakebite protocol

mustKnow.fact: Cobra venom acts after the synapse, and neostigmine given with atropine can improve the weakness. Krait venom acts before the synapse, and neostigmine often does little. A krait bite with failing ventilation is intubated. Anti-snake venom does not immediately reverse paralysis that is already established.
mustKnow.source: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare national snakebite protocol

mustKnow.fact: An arterial tourniquet, cutting the wound, and suction do harm and do not remove venom. The limb is immobilised and the patient is moved. A tourniquet that has been on for a long time is released where a sudden fall in pressure can be treated.
mustKnow.source: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare national snakebite protocol

mustKnow.fact: Indian red scorpion sting causes an autonomic storm and pulmonary oedema. Prazosin 0.5 mg by mouth in an adult, repeated until the extremities are warm and dry, is the treatment. Anti-snake venom has no role. Pulmonary oedema is treated as heart failure, not as a snake bite.
mustKnow.source: Standard Indian scorpion practice

mustKnow.fact: A Hymenoptera sting that causes anaphylaxis is treated with intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg of 1 in 1000 into the thigh, and the airway is watched. An antihistamine is only an adjunct. Many stings without anaphylaxis are a toxic envenoming and can injure the kidney, which is a different illness.
mustKnow.source: Standard anaphylaxis practice
