topics.title: Environmental and drug induced hyperthermia emergencies
topics.book: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 43 Thermoregulatory Disorders; Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Temperature Alterations and High-Altitude Illness

mustKnow.fact: Heat stroke is a core temperature above 40 C with central nervous system dysfunction. Cooling starts at once and is stopped around 38 to 39 C so the patient is not overshot into hypothermia. Exertional heat stroke is cooled in ice water. Classic heat stroke, in an elderly or anticholinergic patient, is cooled by evaporation if immersion is impossible. Antipyretics do not work, because the hypothalamic set point is not the problem.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 43

mustKnow.fact: Swiss stage I hypothermia is a conscious shivering patient from 35 to 32 C. Stage II is impaired consciousness from 32 C down to 28 C. Stage III is unconscious from 28 C down to 24 C. Stage IV is loss of vital signs below 24 C. An Osborn J wave may be present. Handle the patient gently, because a rough move can trigger ventricular fibrillation. In a rescue, death is not declared while the patient is still cold and might be resuscitated, unless the injury is unsurvivable. That rule is not a reason to continue ICU care after a completed warm brain-death examination.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Temperature Alterations

mustKnow.fact: Drowning kills by hypoxia. Ventilation starts as soon as the patient is reached. The cervical spine is immobilised only when the history suggests trauma, such as a dive or a fall. Surfactant washout produces an acute respiratory distress picture, and pulmonary oedema can appear late, so a normal first examination does not send the patient straight home. Abdominal thrusts are not routine.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Temperature Alterations

mustKnow.fact: High-voltage electrical injury is a crush and a burn together. Current across the chest, loss of consciousness, or a voltage above 1000 V is a reason for cardiac monitoring. Rhabdomyolysis and a muscle compartment are sought even when the skin wound is small. Alternating current causes ventricular fibrillation more readily than a single direct-current shock.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 43

mustKnow.fact: Lightning injury is managed with reverse triage. The person who looks dead, in respiratory or cardiac arrest, is treated first, because that arrest is often survivable. Fixed pupils in the first minutes do not by themselves mean brain death. A long resuscitation is reasonable.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Temperature Alterations

mustKnow.fact: Malignant hyperthermia is a hypermetabolic reaction to a volatile anaesthetic or to succinylcholine. The earliest sign is a rising end-tidal carbon dioxide that does not settle with more minute ventilation. The trigger is stopped, and dantrolene is given at 2.5 mg/kg intravenously and repeated until the hypercarbia settles, up to a total around 10 mg/kg. The fever comes later. This is not heat stroke and not sepsis.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 43

mustKnow.fact: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome builds over days, with lead-pipe rigidity and bradyreflexia after an antipsychotic. Serotonin syndrome builds over hours, with clonus and hyperreflexia after a serotonergic drug. The drug is stopped, and benzodiazepines and cooling are used in both. Bromocriptine or dantrolene is for the neuroleptic syndrome. Cyproheptadine, 12 mg as a first dose, is for serotonin syndrome. The two antidotes are not interchangeable.
mustKnow.source: Marino ICU Book 5e Ch. 43

mustKnow.fact: Descent is the treatment of severe high-altitude illness. High-altitude cerebral oedema is given dexamethasone and oxygen while descent is arranged. High-altitude pulmonary oedema is given oxygen and nifedipine, and descent. Acetazolamide prevents acute mountain sickness. It does not replace descent once cerebral or pulmonary oedema is present.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, High-Altitude Illness

topics.title: Obstetric critical care
topics.book: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Maternal-Fetal Critical Care and Preeclampsia and Eclampsia

mustKnow.fact: Severe hypertension in pregnancy, a systolic pressure of 160 mmHg or more or a diastolic pressure of 110 mmHg or more, is treated. The drugs are labetalol, hydralazine, or nifedipine. Labetalol is avoided in asthma. ACE inhibitors are contraindicated before delivery.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Preeclampsia and Eclampsia

mustKnow.fact: Eclampsia is treated with magnesium sulfate, 4 g intravenously as a load and then 1 g per hour, continued for 24 hours after delivery or the last seizure. The infusion stops if the tendon reflexes disappear or the respiratory rate falls below 12 breaths per minute. The antidote is calcium gluconate 1 g intravenously. A further seizure during treatment gets a further magnesium bolus, not a switch to phenytoin.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Preeclampsia and Eclampsia

mustKnow.fact: HELLP is haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets, usually with hypertension. Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is liver failure in the third trimester with hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy, often without dramatic hypertension. Delivery is the treatment of both. Steroids for the fetal lung do not replace delivery of a sick mother.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Maternal-Fetal Critical Care

mustKnow.fact: Postpartum haemorrhage is first tone, then trauma, tissue, and thrombin. Oxytocin is the first uterotonic. The WOMAN trial used tranexamic acid 1 g and reduced death due to bleeding when it was given within 3 hours. The composite primary outcome of death or hysterectomy was not reduced. A second gram is considered if bleeding continues. Tranexamic acid does not replace surgery or blood.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Maternal-Fetal Critical Care

mustKnow.fact: Amniotic fluid embolism presents as sudden hypoxia, hypotension, and disseminated intravascular coagulation during labour or immediately after birth. Treatment is oxygen, circulation, and replacement of blood and clotting factors. There is no specific antidote.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Maternal-Fetal Critical Care

mustKnow.fact: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is new systolic heart failure in the last month of pregnancy or in the months after delivery, with an ejection fraction below 45 percent and no other cause. An ACE inhibitor is avoided before delivery and can start after delivery. Anticoagulation is considered when the ejection fraction is severely reduced, because thrombus is common.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Maternal-Fetal Critical Care

mustKnow.fact: Maternal sepsis gets an antibiotic within 1 hour. The source includes chorioamnionitis, pyelonephritis, and mastitis. An infected uterus is delivered. Until delivery the uterus is displaced to the left so it does not compress the vena cava. Pregnancy is not a reason to water down the sepsis bundle.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Maternal-Fetal Critical Care

mustKnow.fact: If a pregnant woman whose fundus is at or above the umbilicus, about 20 weeks, has no return of circulation by about 4 minutes, a resuscitative hysterotomy starts where she lies, aiming to deliver by about 5 minutes. The aim is to relieve aortocaval compression and help the mother. Left uterine displacement is used until the incision. She is not moved to a theatre first.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Maternal-Fetal Critical Care

modules.name: Critically ill cancer and immunocompromised patient

topics.title: Critically ill cancer and immunocompromised patient
topics.book: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Oncologic Emergencies

mustKnow.fact: Tumour lysis syndrome is two or more of a high uric acid, a high potassium, a high phosphate, and a low calcium, from a tumour that is breaking down. Clinical lysis adds kidney injury, an arrhythmia, or a seizure. Rasburicase, about 0.2 mg/kg, destroys uric acid that is already present. Allopurinol only stops new uric acid being made, and it is the drug when G6PD deficiency rules out rasburicase, because rasburicase causes haemolysis in that deficiency. Calcium is given only for tetany or an arrhythmia, because it precipitates with phosphate. Hydration is the other half of treatment.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Oncologic Emergencies

mustKnow.fact: Neutropenic sepsis is fever when the neutrophil count is below 500 per microlitre, or is about to fall after cytotoxic treatment. An antipseudomonal beta-lactam is given within 1 hour. Do not wait for the count if that history is clear. Vancomycin is added for a suspicious line, severe mucositis, known resistant gram-positive infection, or shock. It is not automatic for every fever.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Oncologic Emergencies

mustKnow.fact: Cytokine release syndrome after CAR-T cell therapy is fever, then hypotension or hypoxia. Grade 2 or higher is treated with tocilizumab. Immune effector cell neurotoxicity is confusion, speech loss, or seizures, and it is treated with a corticosteroid. Tocilizumab does not usefully enter the brain, so it is not the treatment of that neurotoxicity. This use is separate from tocilizumab in viral pneumonia.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Oncologic Emergencies

mustKnow.fact: Leukostasis is sludging in the lungs and brain. It is more likely above a white cell count of 100 x 10^9 per litre in acute myeloid leukaemia, and at higher counts in lymphoblastic leukaemia. Red cells are not transfused before the count falls, because they raise viscosity. Hydroxyurea or induction chemotherapy is the treatment. Leukapheresis is for symptoms, not for a number alone.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Oncologic Emergencies

mustKnow.fact: Differentiation syndrome from all-trans retinoic acid or arsenic trioxide causes fever, weight gain, pulmonary infiltrates, and hypotension in acute promyelocytic leukaemia. Dexamethasone 10 mg every 12 hours is started. The differentiating drug continues unless the reaction is immediately life-threatening. Stopping it casually lets the leukaemia return.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Oncologic Emergencies

mustKnow.fact: Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis is fever, cytopenias, a high triglyceride or a low fibrinogen, and often haemophagocytosis, driven by a cytokine storm. A ferritin above 10000 ng/mL supports the diagnosis and does not prove it in an adult with sepsis or liver failure. Severe disease is treated with etoposide and dexamethasone, and the trigger, infection or lymphoma, is treated at the same time.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Oncologic Emergencies

mustKnow.fact: Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage gives infiltrates and a falling haemoglobin, and lavage becomes bloodier with each aliquot. Engraftment syndrome is fever, rash, and capillary leak as the neutrophil count recovers after a stem cell transplant. Both can look like infection. A corticosteroid is used once cultures are sent and infection is being treated, not instead of that search.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Oncologic Emergencies

mustKnow.fact: A time-limited trial names the treatment, the outcome that would count as benefit, and the day the team and the family will look again. It is for a real but uncertain chance of recovery, such as a first episode of organ failure in a new cancer. It is not an open-ended promise, and it is not a way to avoid saying that a treatment cannot work.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Oncologic Emergencies

modules.name: Postoperative and cardiac surgical critical care

topics.title: Postoperative and cardiac surgical critical care
topics.book: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e shock, bleeding, and arrhythmia chapters, plus standard cardiac surgical ICU practice. Neither primary manual has a post-cardiotomy chapter.

mustKnow.fact: Bleeding after cardiac surgery is a chest drain that keeps putting out blood, above about 200 mL in an hour, or a drain that stops suddenly while filling pressures rise and the blood pressure falls. The second pattern is tamponade, including a clot that echocardiography can miss. The treatment is re-exploration. More plasma does not fix a surgical bleed.
mustKnow.source: Standard cardiac surgical ICU practice

mustKnow.fact: Low cardiac output after bypass is a cardiac index below 2.2 L/min/m2 with cold extremities and a rising lactate. Bradycardia is paced before a drug is added. An inotrope comes after filling is adequate. Mechanical support is considered when drugs do not restore perfusion. A vasoconstrictor alone, in a cold heart that cannot eject, only raises afterload.
mustKnow.source: Standard cardiac surgical ICU practice

mustKnow.fact: Vasoplegia is hypotension with a high cardiac output and a low systemic vascular resistance. The patient is warm and vasodilated. Noradrenaline is first, and vasopressin is added. Methylene blue is rescue only. It is avoided in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency and in a patient on a serotonergic drug.
mustKnow.source: Standard cardiac surgical ICU practice

mustKnow.fact: Atrial fibrillation after cardiac surgery usually appears from day 2 to day 4. A stable patient is rate-controlled with a beta blocker if the heart is not in shock. Amiodarone is used when a beta blocker is unsafe. Cardioversion is for instability. Anticoagulation weighs stroke risk against fresh suture lines and is not automatic in the first hours.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, arrhythmia chapters

mustKnow.fact: Epicardial pacing wires treat bradycardia and heart block after valve surgery. Loss of capture in a pacing-dependent patient is an emergency: check the connections, then the heart. The wires are not removed while the patient still needs them. When they are removed later, tamponade is the complication that is watched for.
mustKnow.source: Standard cardiac surgical ICU practice

mustKnow.fact: Preventive non-invasive ventilation, started before a high-risk patient tires, can prevent reintubation after major surgery. The same support started only after post-extubation respiratory failure is established can delay reintubation and cause harm. The difference is the timing.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, respiratory failure chapters

mustKnow.fact: Goal-directed fluid in the operating room gives a bolus only while stroke volume still rises, and stops when it does not. It is a way to avoid both hypovolaemia and a drowned patient. It is not a prescription for a positive balance the next day.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, functional haemodynamic monitoring

mustKnow.fact: Enhanced recovery after surgery, once the patient is in the ICU, is warmth, multimodal analgesia so the patient can cough, early enteral intake, and removal of lines that are no longer needed. A cold, fluid-loaded, deeply sedated patient is the pattern these steps replace.
mustKnow.source: Standard perioperative ICU practice

topics.title: Organ transplant critical care
topics.book: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Management of the Solid Organ Transplant Recipient

mustKnow.fact: Primary non-function of a liver graft is failure in the first days, with rising lactate, coagulopathy, and hypoglycaemia, while Doppler shows a patent hepatic artery. Early hepatic artery thrombosis produces the same blood tests and the artery is not patent. Thrombosis goes back to theatre. Non-function needs retransplantation. The Doppler is done before the two are confused.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Management of the Solid Organ Transplant Recipient

mustKnow.fact: Hepatic artery thrombosis also threatens the bile duct later, as ischaemic cholangiopathy, even if the artery was reopened. A rising bilirubin weeks afterwards is not labelled rejection until the artery and the ducts have been imaged.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Management of the Solid Organ Transplant Recipient

mustKnow.fact: Delayed graft function of a kidney is the need for dialysis in the first 7 days and is usually tubular injury from ischaemia. Hypotension and nephrotoxins are avoided. If function does not return, a biopsy looks for rejection, and the calcineurin inhibitor level is checked rather than guessed.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Management of the Solid Organ Transplant Recipient

mustKnow.fact: Primary graft dysfunction of a lung is bilateral infiltrates and poor gas exchange within 72 hours, not explained by rejection, infection, or cardiogenic oedema. A PaO2/FiO2 below 200 is the severe grade. Ventilation is lung protective, and extracorporeal support is used when that fails.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Management of the Solid Organ Transplant Recipient

mustKnow.fact: Hyperacute rejection is preformed antibody attacking the graft within minutes, and the graft is removed. Acute cellular rejection is T-cell injury over days to weeks and is treated by increasing immunosuppression. They are not the same process.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Management of the Solid Organ Transplant Recipient

mustKnow.fact: Calcineurin inhibitor neurotoxicity causes tremor and posterior reversible encephalopathy, with visual change, seizures, and posterior changes on MRI. The blood level is checked, the blood pressure is treated, and the drug is reduced or switched. It is not a stroke for thrombolysis.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Management of the Solid Organ Transplant Recipient

mustKnow.fact: Infections follow a rough calendar. In the first month they are bacterial, surgical, or donor-derived. From month 1 to month 6 they are opportunistic, including cytomegalovirus and Pneumocystis. After prophylaxis stops, community infection and late cytomegalovirus appear. Co-trimoxazole is not omitted for convenience. A fever is not called rejection until infection has been considered.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Management of the Solid Organ Transplant Recipient

mustKnow.fact: Maintenance immunosuppression is usually a calcineurin inhibitor, an antimetabolite, and a steroid. The inhibitor injures the kidney, the antimetabolite suppresses marrow and gut, and the steroid raises glucose. All three are not stopped because of a fever. Stopping them causes rejection, which is then mistaken for worsening infection.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Management of the Solid Organ Transplant Recipient

topics.title: ICU procedures
topics.book: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Procedures; Marino ICU Book 5e, vascular access

mustKnow.fact: An internal jugular central venous catheter is placed under ultrasound. The wire is seen in the vein before any dilator is passed. If a large dilator has already entered the carotid artery, it is not pulled out on the ward. That hole needs surgical repair.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Central Venous Catheterization

mustKnow.fact: The 3SITES trial found a lower composite of bloodstream infection and symptomatic thrombosis with the subclavian vein than with the jugular or femoral vein, at the cost of more pneumothorax. A patient with bad clotting still gets a vein that can be compressed. The trial is a default, not a site that ignores the lungs.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Central Venous Catheterization

mustKnow.fact: A radial arterial cannula is transduced at the phlebostatic axis, the 4th intercostal space at the mid thorax. A dampened trace underestimates systolic pressure. The Allen test does not reliably predict hand ischaemia and does not delay the line in an unstable patient.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Arterial Catheterization

mustKnow.fact: Percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy is elective, guided by bronchoscopy, and sited at tracheal ring 2 to ring 4, not through the cricoid and not as an emergency airway. Coagulopathy and very high ventilator pressures raise the risk. The same bronchoscopy clears a mucus plug and takes a directed lavage, and the airway stays secure throughout.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Percutaneous Tracheostomy

mustKnow.fact: A chest drain sits in the triangle of safety, just above a rib, after a finger sweep, on an underwater seal. A bubbling drain is never clamped. A tube that has slipped out is not pushed back in. Needle decompression of tension pneumothorax uses the 4th or 5th intercostal space in the anterior axillary line. The 2nd intercostal space in the midclavicular line is an alternative. A short needle fails in a thick chest, so a drain follows.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Chest Tube Insertion

mustKnow.fact: Lumbar puncture is avoided when a mass is causing midline shift, when the skin is infected, or when a coagulopathy is uncorrected. Opening pressure is measured in the lateral position. A postural headache afterwards is not meningitis unless fever or a falling conscious level says otherwise.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Lumbar Puncture

mustKnow.fact: Pericardiocentesis for tamponade is guided by echocardiography. In cardiac arrest the approach is subxiphoid. Blood from a cardiac chamber clots in the bowl. Blood that has sat in the pericardium often does not. Pulsus paradoxus, distended neck veins, and chamber collapse support the diagnosis before the needle.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Procedures

mustKnow.fact: Diagnostic paracentesis in cirrhosis is not delayed to correct a moderately raised INR. The bleed from the tap is less dangerous than missing infected ascites. When more than 5 litres are removed, albumin is given at about 6 to 8 g per litre removed. The central line bundle, separately, is hand hygiene, chlorhexidine, a maximal sterile barrier, avoiding the femoral vein when a safer site exists, and a daily decision to remove the line.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual of Critical Care 4e, Paracentesis

modules.name: Ethics, end of life care and communication

topics.title: Ethics, end of life care and communication
topics.book: Common Cause judgment, 2018, procedure simplified in 2023; Washington Manual end-of-life practice where it matches. Indian law is not in the Washington chapter.

mustKnow.fact: Withholding a treatment and withdrawing it are the same ethical decision. What differs is how it feels to the family. Opioids and benzodiazepines titrated to pain or breathlessness are continued. At those doses they are not active euthanasia. The aim is relief, and the dose is not increased in order to end life.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual end-of-life practice

mustKnow.fact: The Common Cause judgment of 2018 recognised passive euthanasia and an advance medical directive in India. A 2023 order simplified how a directive is recorded and how hospital boards review a decision. Active euthanasia remains illegal. A directive that is already in the record is followed. It does not have to be rediscovered during the emergency.
mustKnow.source: Common Cause judgment, 2018, procedure simplified in 2023

mustKnow.fact: Capacity is judged for the decision in front of the team, not as a permanent label. A patient who can understand, retain, weigh, and state the choice is the decision maker. When nobody can consent and the need is immediate, treatment proceeds in the patient's best interests and is documented. A relative is consulted when present. A relative does not overrule a capable patient.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual end-of-life practice

mustKnow.fact: Physiological futility means a treatment cannot achieve its biological aim, such as restarting a heart that will not restart. That treatment may be withheld, and the reason is explained. Futility is not a claim that the person's life has no value. Disagreement is met with a second opinion and a time-limited trial, not with a silent stop and not with endless escalation.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual end-of-life practice

mustKnow.fact: A family meeting uses one spokesperson, a plain account of what is wrong and what is likely, and a medical recommendation. The useful question is what the patient would have wanted. Offering a menu of futile options as if they were equal is not shared decision making. The meeting is written in the notes.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual end-of-life practice

mustKnow.fact: When beds or ventilators are scarce, triage follows the likelihood of benefit from intensive care. It is not first come, and it is not age by itself. A patient who is not admitted still receives care, including palliative care. Triage is not abandonment.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual end-of-life practice

mustKnow.fact: Informed consent for a procedure covers the purpose, the important risks, the alternatives, and the option of not doing it. It is taken from a capable patient or the rightful surrogate. Emergency implied consent is written down as soon as the procedure is done. A signature on a form the patient could not understand is not consent.
mustKnow.source: Washington Manual end-of-life practice

mustKnow.fact: News of dying is given in plain words, without a euphemism that hides death. The organ donation conversation is separate from the news of death, and a refusal does not change symptom control. The legal tests for brainstem death belong to that topic. They are not reused as a bargaining step.
mustKnow.source: Common Cause judgment and Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues practice

topics.title: ICU organisation, quality and safety
topics.book: NEWS2 (Royal College of Physicians); NHSN ventilator-associated event framework; SCCM staffing statements. No organisation chapter in Marino 5e or Washington Manual 4e.

mustKnow.fact: A closed ICU is one in which the intensivist writes the orders. Observational comparisons associate that model with better outcomes. An open unit, where every parent team writes its own critical care, fragments the plan. A title on the door, without the authority to change the ventilator, is not a closed unit.
mustKnow.source: SCCM staffing statements

mustKnow.fact: The MERIT trial introduced a medical emergency team and did not significantly reduce the composite of cardiac arrest, unplanned ICU admission, and unexpected death. Calling criteria are still widely used. The trial is a reason not to claim a mortality benefit it did not show.
mustKnow.source: MERIT trial, Lancet 2005

mustKnow.fact: A NEWS2 total of 7 or more is the high-risk band and needs an emergency response. A score of 3 in one parameter needs urgent review even when the total looks moderate. Scale 2, for a patient at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, sets the oxygen saturation target at 88 to 92 percent. Scale 1 is the default.
mustKnow.source: Royal College of Physicians NEWS2

mustKnow.fact: In the NHSN framework a ventilator-associated condition is a rise in the daily minimum FiO2 of 0.20 or more, or in PEEP of 3 cmH2O or more, sustained for 2 calendar days after a stable baseline. An infection-related ventilator-associated complication adds abnormal temperature or white cell count and a new antibiotic. This is surveillance. It is not the same as a clinical pneumonia, and it is not by itself a reason to start antibiotics.
mustKnow.source: NHSN ventilator-associated event framework

mustKnow.fact: The Michigan Keystone programme used a central-line checklist and a rule that any member of the team could stop the procedure when a step was missed. Catheter bloodstream infections fell. It was a collaborative, not a randomised trial. The steps remain hand hygiene, chlorhexidine, a full barrier, a safer site, and removal of the line.
mustKnow.source: Michigan Keystone ICU project

mustKnow.fact: Handover uses ISBAR: identity, situation, background, assessment, and recommendation. A list of drugs with no plan loses the sickest problem. The incoming clinician repeats that problem back.
mustKnow.source: Standard ICU safety practice

mustKnow.fact: Tele-ICU lets an intensivist review a remote unit and support the local nurse and doctor. It does not see the skin, the family, or a displaced tube as well as the person at the bedside. The bedside check still happens.
mustKnow.source: SCCM staffing statements

mustKnow.fact: A daily goals sheet states the sedation target, the ventilation plan, the feeding plan, and which lines and drugs can stop. A pharmacist on the round catches dose errors. These are safety practices, not paperwork for its own sake.
mustKnow.source: Standard ICU safety practice

topics.title: ICU-acquired complications and rehabilitation
topics.book: TEAM trial, NEJM 2022; post-intensive care follow-up practice

mustKnow.fact: Post-intensive care syndrome is a new or worse impairment of the body, of cognition, or of mental health that persists after critical illness. Families can develop anxiety, depression, and complicated grief, the family form of the same syndrome. It is sought after discharge. It is not a diagnosis made on the day of admission.
mustKnow.source: Post-intensive care follow-up practice

mustKnow.fact: The TEAM trial compared a higher dose of early active mobilisation with usual mobilisation. Days alive and out of hospital at 180 days were a median of 143 with the higher dose and 145 with usual care, not a significant gain. Adverse events, including arrhythmia, a blood pressure swing, and desaturation, were more common with the higher dose. Usual mobilisation continues. The trial argues against an aggressive dose in an unstable patient, not against sitting up.
mustKnow.source: TEAM trial, NEJM 2022

mustKnow.fact: The physical part of post-intensive care syndrome is often ICU-acquired weakness. An MRC sum score below 48 out of 60, when the patient can be tested, marks it. Lighter sedation and less paralysis are the prevention. No drug reverses the weakness after it is established.
mustKnow.source: Post-intensive care follow-up practice

mustKnow.fact: Pressure injury is prevented by repositioning and by offloading devices, including the mask, the tube ties, and lines. An ulcer under a device is still a pressure injury. It is recorded as a safety event.
mustKnow.source: Post-intensive care follow-up practice

mustKnow.fact: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis is low-molecular-weight heparin while bleeding allows it. The PROTECT trial found fewer pulmonary emboli with dalteparin than with unfractionated heparin, and no mortality difference. Mechanical compression is the bridge while anticoagulation is unsafe, and it is not a permanent substitute once bleeding has stopped.
mustKnow.source: PROTECT trial

mustKnow.fact: Stress ulcer prophylaxis is for the patient who is ventilated or coagulopathic, and it stops when that risk stops. SUP-ICU found that pantoprazole did not reduce 90 day mortality and did reduce clinically important bleeding. A proton pump inhibitor continued onto the ward with no indication is not what the trial supports.
mustKnow.source: SUP-ICU trial

mustKnow.fact: Follow-up asks about memory, concentration, mood, and nightmares. Post-traumatic stress disorder and cognitive impairment are common and are missed if the only question is about the wound. A follow-up clinic is the structure that catches them.
mustKnow.source: Post-intensive care follow-up practice

mustKnow.fact: An ICU diary may help a patient make sense of delusions. The evidence is mixed, and a diary is not a treatment for weakness or for post-traumatic stress disorder by itself. Rehabilitation begins with sitting and range of movement when the patient is stable, timed with the sedation break. It is not the high-dose TEAM protocol on the first unstable day.
mustKnow.source: TEAM trial, NEJM 2022

topics.title: Landmark trials in critical care
topics.book: Primary reports of the named trials. This topic teaches the endpoint, not a slogan.

mustKnow.fact: ARDSNet ARMA compared 6 mL/kg predicted body weight with 12 mL/kg, and kept plateau pressure at or below 30 cmH2O. The lower tidal volume reduced mortality. Predicted body weight is used, not the weight on the bed.
mustKnow.source: ARDSNet ARMA, NEJM 2000

mustKnow.fact: PROSEVA gave prone positioning for at least 16 hours when PaO2/FiO2 was below 150 mmHg, in units that already used a low tidal volume. Mortality fell. Prone position was a treatment, not a last-minute turn.
mustKnow.source: PROSEVA, NEJM 2013

mustKnow.fact: NICE-SUGAR compared a glucose target of 81 to 108 mg/dL with a target of 180 mg/dL or below. The tighter target increased 90 day mortality, and severe hypoglycaemia was more common. Tight control at 81 to 108 is not the ICU default.
mustKnow.source: NICE-SUGAR, NEJM 2009

mustKnow.fact: TRICC found that a transfusion threshold of 7 g/dL was not worse than 10 g/dL in euvolaemic critically ill adults, and was better in those who were less severely ill. SAFE found that 4 percent albumin did not change 28 day mortality overall compared with saline, and albumin was associated with higher mortality in traumatic brain injury. Neither result makes albumin, or a haemoglobin of 10, the routine.
mustKnow.source: TRICC, NEJM 1999; SAFE, NEJM 2004

mustKnow.fact: The 6S trial found that hydroxyethyl starch increased 90 day mortality and the need for renal replacement compared with Ringer's acetate in sepsis. Starch is not an ICU resuscitation fluid.
mustKnow.source: 6S trial, NEJM 2012

mustKnow.fact: ProCESS, ARISE, and ProMISe found that protocolised early goal-directed therapy did not reduce mortality compared with usual care that already gave early antibiotics and attention to lactate. The original Rivers protocol is not the standard.
mustKnow.source: ProCESS, NEJM 2014; ARISE, NEJM 2014; ProMISe, NEJM 2015

mustKnow.fact: ADRENAL gave hydrocortisone 200 mg per day in septic shock and did not reduce 90 day mortality. Shock reversed faster. HYPRESS found that steroids did not stop severe sepsis from progressing to shock. Steroids are for refractory shock, not for every infection.
mustKnow.source: ADRENAL, NEJM 2018; HYPRESS, JAMA 2016

mustKnow.fact: TTM2 found that cooling to 33 C after cardiac arrest did not reduce death at 6 months compared with active prevention of fever. The cooled patients had more haemodynamic instability. The task is to prevent fever, not to chase 33 C in every survivor.
mustKnow.source: TTM2, NEJM 2021

mustKnow.fact: SMART found that balanced crystalloid reduced the 30 day composite of death, new dialysis, or persistent kidney dysfunction compared with saline. CLOVERS found no 90 day mortality difference between a restrictive and a liberal fluid strategy after the initial sepsis resuscitation. A balanced fluid is reasonable. Neither trial is a licence for unlimited volume, and saline is not banned.
mustKnow.source: SMART, NEJM 2018; CLOVERS, NEJM 2023

mustKnow.fact: STARRT-AKI found that accelerated renal replacement did not reduce 90 day mortality and left more survivors dependent on dialysis. Emergency indications, a dangerous potassium, severe acidosis, pulmonary oedema, a dialysable toxin, or uraemic complications, are still not a reason to wait.
mustKnow.source: STARRT-AKI, NEJM 2020

mustKnow.fact: EOLIA compared venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, with crossover from conventional care allowed, in very severe ARDS. The primary 60 day mortality result was not statistically significant. Enrolment included a PaO2/FiO2 below 50 for more than 3 hours or below 80 for more than 6 hours. A non-significant primary result with crossover is not proof that the circuit does nothing, and it is not an indication for every patient with ARDS.
mustKnow.source: EOLIA, NEJM 2018

mustKnow.fact: FLORALI found that high-flow nasal oxygen lowered 90 day mortality in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure compared with standard oxygen or non-invasive ventilation. Intubation by day 28, the primary endpoint, was not clearly reduced in the whole cohort. The mortality result and the intubation result are reported as they were, not merged into one slogan.
mustKnow.source: FLORALI, NEJM 2015

mustKnow.fact: RECOVERY showed that dexamethasone 6 mg daily for up to 10 days reduced 28 day mortality in COVID-19 when the patient needed oxygen or ventilation. Patients breathing room air were not helped. The steroid does not replace a tidal volume of 6 mL/kg predicted body weight or a plateau pressure at or below 30 cmH2O.
mustKnow.source: RECOVERY, NEJM 2021

mustKnow.fact: A negative primary endpoint is not rescued by a favourable subgroup that was not prespecified, and crossover, as in EOLIA, means the control arm is no longer pure conventional care. These trials are memorised by the direction of the primary result. A later lesson that quotes only the slogan will get the mark wrong.
mustKnow.source: How to read the trials named in this topic
